The problems of the kit (a model that cannot be read, without triangles, too heavy) are shown at the top of the panel.

The bands of the kit are laid along the facade, in place of the bands WorldMint makes: the base at the bottom, all around the building, cut at the doors; the string course where the recipe has a band (the closest in height, if there are several); the cornice at the top, where the recipe has a cornice. Each keeps the height of its model, is repeated per bay (stretched to fit) and mitred at the corners. Without a band of a role, the made band stays.

Save the kit writes kit.json in the folder; the old one is kept as kit.json.bak. A file is not a step of the history: Ctrl+Z does not undo it.

What is measured, when the kit is read: the size of each model turned towards the street, its triangles (above the limit for a kit piece, it is simplified), and its plain wall, the part of its wall plane that reaches its edges. What is not: its role, its front and its materials, which only you describe. To fill a cell larger or smaller than itself, a model with plain wall around its opening stretches in nine cells: only the wall bands grow or shrink, the opening, its frame and its mouldings keep their size, and the brick keeps its density. Without plain wall, the model stretches as one block, by at most the Allowed stretch; beyond that, the cell keeps the made module.

For now, the kit is described, read and checked (city_check reports a kit with a problem); placing its pieces on the buildings comes in a later version.

items.title: The game map
items.text: The Make the game map button, under the plan view in the Cities and roads section, writes the image of the plan seen from above (the districts in the colour of their style, the painted paths in the shade of their material, the sidewalks and roadways in light greys, without text) to cartes/plan_ville.png, in the project folder. If the game has the Map system, the image becomes its drawn map, with the area it covers: the game minimap shows the city, north up. It is one step: Ctrl+Z brings back the previous map. Without the Map system, the image is only written, and the log says so. Make the map again after changing the city.

items.title: Shortcuts
items.text: Gesture In Streets mode In Districts mode Click on the ground Places a point of the street Places a point of the area Enter, double click Ends the street Closes the area Right click while drawing Removes the last point Removes the last point Escape Drops the drawing, or clears the choice; otherwise puts the tool away Same Click on a street, a district Chooses the street Chooses the district Drag a node, a point Moves the street (a single step) Changes the district's shape Right click on a street, a junction, a district Profile, name, delete; roundabout Style, name, another draw, delete; remove or add a point Delete Deletes the chosen street Deletes the chosen district Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y Undo, redo Undo, redo

items.title: With the agent
items.text:
The agent works on the same plan as you, with its own tools:

Agent tool What it does city_generate Generates a whole city (a size, districts, a seed). It asks you before replacing yours. It also lays out a town in a zone (an outline, or a turned rectangle), with its ambiance and its name, next to the others. In a scene without terrain, it makes a flat ground under the city, in the same step (one Ctrl+Z removes both); the ground materials the city turns on (its grass, its painted paths) enter the project in that same step. city_town_set Renames a town, lays it out again in its zone with another seed (in a scene without terrain, it first makes the same flat ground as city_generate), or deletes it. city_road_add Adds a street between two places or two nodes, with a profile and a name. city_road_set Changes the profile, the name or the path of a street, deletes it; turns a junction into a roundabout; forces its upkeep (new, worn, cracked, patched) or gives it back to the district; chooses the material and the tint of a part of this street only (materials). It can also refuse a bridge on a street. city_get Reads the plan: the streets, the junctions, the districts and the styles; counts the blocks, the parcels and the buildings (landmarks, changed, locked, mean and highest floors per style), lists the parcels of a street and describes one building. city_check Looks for what is wrong: an unwanted dead end, a slope too steep, two streets crossing without a junction, a section too short, a parcel without access; and for buildings: an unknown facade recipe or wall material, a facade kit that cannot be read, a parcel too shallow for a building, a building buried in the slope, the missing model of a landmark, a building too detailed for its triangle budget. city_district_set Draws a district, changes its style, its name or its outline, redraws it, deletes it. city_style_set Creates or sets a district style (with the states and materials of its streets, the materials of its facades and its grime decal, grimeDecal) or a street profile (its lanes, edges, markings, materials and their states). A project material can come from the online library: the agent searches it with library_search and adds it with library_add, on the sources you chose. city_building_set Changes a parcel and its building: leave it free, build on it, give it another style; the floors, the roof, the facade, the wall, the tint, the shift, the shop; the slabs of its ground (their material, their height, an added slab); lock it as it is; replace it with a landmark (a model of the project, or the parcel left empty). It changes one remarkable building at a time: for a whole district, it changes the style. It reattaches or removes a change that no longer fits. city_shop_kind_set The catalogue of the kinds of shops: with no argument, the list (shown name, corner use, name patterns, logo, hours, floor, interior recipe) and how many shops of each kind the city has; a kind and its values change it or add one ("librairie"); an added kind can be removed. A single shop is renamed with city_building_set (shopName, shopLogo, visitable). city_shop_kind_set The catalogue of the kinds of shops: with no argument, the list (shown name, corner use, name patterns, logo, hours) and how many shops of each kind the city has; a kind and its values change it or add one ("librairie"); an added kind can be removed. A single shop is renamed with city_building_set (shopName, shopLogo, visitable). city_storefront_set The storefront styles: with no argument, the list (name, colours, params) and how many shops of the city take each; a style and its values change it or add one (from: copied from another); an added style can be removed. A single shop changes its storefront with city_building_set (storefront). city_kit_set Describes a facade kit: without kit, lists the models of the folder (size, triangles, material names) and the current kit.json; with kit, writes kit.json (the old one kept as kit.json.bak). Like Describe the kit…: nothing is guessed from a name, and it is not an undoable step.

Each of its gestures is one step, undone with Ctrl+Z. It checks its work by looking at images of the city.

A few requests: "Generate a medium city with a port and an old town", "An avenue from the port to the hill", "Make the town hall junction a roundabout", "The suburban houses to the north, more spread out", "Put the town hall on the corner of the square, and lock the building opposite".

items.title: What is saved
items.text:
The plan (streets, districts, styles, profiles) is saved in the scene. The roadway is stored in the project folder (.worldmint/ville/) and taken along by the export: an exported game shows the city without the extension. Outside a project, the streets only show as lines.

The roadway, the sidewalks and the bridges are objects produced by the extension: they can be seen and chosen in the scene, but not moved or deleted by hand. To change them, change the plan, with the Cities and roads tool.

items.title: A paid extension
items.text:
Cities and roads is a paid extension of WorldMint. What stays in the free engine:

  • games: a game made with the city plays and exports everywhere, without the extension;
  • scenes: a scene that has a city also opens without the extension; the roadway shows, and the city's plan is kept intact;
  • the generic hooks the extension uses (tools added to the editor and the agent, produced objects stored in the project, areas where the terrain sows no plants, a framed top view): they serve every extension, and are described in Writing an extension.

Today, the extension opens as soon as it is installed. Later, it will depend on the licence of your WorldMint account; without a licence, the editor will say so once at startup, and the city's data will stay kept in your scenes.

items.title: Known limits
items.text:
• No buildings yet. The districts and their styles prepare the parcels and what will be built on them, but the buildings are not built yet.
  • A district drawn larger than its streets keeps parcels on the outer side of its edge streets (a generated city stops at the centre line of its edge streets).
  • Changes that no longer fit: their buttons can be half cut off at the bottom of the panel.
  • Two avenue junctions very close together (about twenty metres) can give a tight join: move them apart.
  • In the plan view, the names of two neighbouring streets can overlap.

items.title: Game controls
items.text:
Controls are the game's keys: one control per player action. They are set in Developer mode, in the Game controls panel (the Game controls button at the top of the Systems panel, or the Windows menu), and apply to the whole game.

Each control has:

  • a label, which the player sees ("Jump");
  • a name for scripts (jump): scripts and systems ask "is the jump control pressed?", never a precise key. Changing the key therefore breaks nothing;
  • a key (or a mouse button, or the wheel);
  • a gamepad button, optional.

When you hover over a label, the editor shows the name for scripts and where the control comes from: this game, the engine, or the system that added it.

items.title: Starting controls
items.text:
A new game has these controls. The first seven come from the engine; Attack and Use belong to the game, which can remove them.

Control Name for scripts Key Gamepad Move forward move_forward W (Z on an AZERTY keyboard) left stick Move back move_back S left stick Move left move_left A (Q on an AZERTY keyboard) left stick Move right move_right D left stick Run run Left Shift LT Jump jump Space A Pause pause Esc Start Attack attack Click X Use interact E Y

Keys are read by their place on the keyboard, not by their letter: the editor shows the letter of your keyboard (Z on AZERTY, where QWERTY has W). The gamepad's right stick turns the camera.

Some systems add their own when you activate them: Block (block, right-click, LB) with Basic combat, Drink a potion (heal, R, ↑) with Healing. See the systems reference.

items.title: Changing a key
items.text:
1. Click the key button, to the right of the label: it shows "Press a key…".
  2. Press the key, mouse button or wheel notch you want. Escape cancels.

The list next to it chooses the gamepad button (None for no button): A, B, X, Y, LB, RB, LT, RT, Start, Back, L3, R3 and the four arrows.

Changing a control of a system or of the engine keeps it in this game, with the new key. Ctrl+Z goes back.

items.title: Adding a control
items.text:
Add a control opens a small form:

  • Name for scripts: a word without spaces (open_map);
  • Label for the player: "Open the map";
  • Key: click, then press the key.

Add creates it ("This name is already taken." if a control already has this name). A script then reads it with game.pressed("open_map"): see the scripts reference.

The Remove this control cross deletes a control that belongs to the game. Engine and system controls cannot be removed: if you changed their key, removing it gives them back their starting key.

items.title: In the game
items.text:
• The mouse turns the camera. When the game shows a cursor (an inventory, a menu), it is used to click.
  • Esc is the Pause control: if no script uses it, it frees the mouse, to click outside the window or close it. A click in the window takes the mouse back.
  • When a game ends (won or lost), the screen shows "R: play again Esc: quit".
  • A connected gamepad is picked up at once; the game then shows the gamepad's buttons in its prompts.
  • The game's windows (menus, dialogues, inventory, shop, quest log) work with a gamepad and a keyboard: the d-pad, the left stick or the arrow keys move from one button to another, A or Enter clicks, B or Escape closes. While a window is used that way, these buttons do not fire their control (A does not jump). See Gamepad and keyboard.
  • A script can let the player change their keys during the game (game.bind).

items.title: Quality
items.text:
Quality sets how detailed the picture is: shadows, lights, water, the glow around strong lights, and how far the terrain and plants keep their detail. It has three levels.

Level What changes For whom Low Blurrier shadows up close (3 maps of 1,024 pixels), 256 lights at once, simpler water (no refraction), smaller glow, detailed terrain up to 512 m, plants up to 60% of their distance, fewer particles at once (in the game). An integrated graphics chip (most laptops). Medium Shadows almost as sharp as High (3 maps of 2,048 pixels instead of 4), 512 lights at once and fewer light shadows, water like High, a glow as wide but computed smaller, detailed terrain up to 768 m, plants up to 80% of their distance. The editor's views, by default; a player whose graphics card struggles. High The finest everywhere: 4 shadow maps of 2,048 pixels, 1,024 lights, water with refraction and scenery reflections, detailed terrain up to 1,024 m, plants at their full distance. A graphics card: the game's picture as you want it. Ultra High, taken further: the full detail of imported models (facade kits, trees, cars) up to twice as far before their simplified version, their draw ranges and the merged districts half as far again, shadow maps of 4,096 pixels, detailed terrain up to 1,536 m, plants a quarter further, finer fog and rays. A powerful graphics card (above the RTX 4070 class). The game's target stays Medium (RTX 4060 class).

items.title: Where to set it
items.text:
• For the editor's views: Preferences, Display section, View quality (Medium at first). It only applies to you, in the editor. A scene's Shadow quality (Sky and light) never goes above it there.
  • For the game: it chooses at startup, from the player's computer (Low on an integrated chip, High on a graphics card). The game started with Play does the same: it does not take the editor's view quality.
  • For the player: with the Menu system, Options, Graphics, Quality (see below).

items.title: The editor's views only work when the picture changes
items.text: Whatever the quality, the editor only redraws a view when its picture would change: the camera moves, an object changes, a view setting changes, or something moves on its own (visible water, particles, terrain that is still arriving). Otherwise the view keeps its previous picture. While you type a message to the agent, or while the agent works, the views cost almost nothing. With four views, the ones that are neither under the mouse nor being edited follow an object you move a little less often (20 times per second), and water 10 times per second; the view under the mouse follows everything at every frame (water, 30 times per second).

items.title: Upscaling
items.text:
Upscaling draws the scene in an image smaller than the window, then enlarges it to the window's size. So as not to lose detail, it shifts the camera very slightly at every frame (by a fraction of a pixel) and blends the frames that follow one another: within a few frames, it knows more than a single frame shows. Object edges no longer look jagged ("staircase" edges), and the graphics card has fewer pixels to compute.

What enlarges the picture is the upscaling method:

  • None (default): WorldMint's own computation, on every graphics card;
  • FSR (all cards): AMD FSR 2, sharper, especially when the picture is much reduced; it works on every card and is already in WorldMint (see AMD FSR);
  • DLSS (NVIDIA): on NVIDIA GeForce RTX cards, if you provided it (see NVIDIA DLSS).

Where the chosen method doesn't work, WorldMint's replaces it, without telling the player.

items.title: Where to set it
items.text:
• For the game: nothing selected, Game window section, Upscaling (the level) and Upscaling method. The setting goes with the exported game. The agent can change it too (except choosing DLSS).
  • For the editor's views: Preferences, Display section, View upscaling and View upscaling method. It only applies to you, in the editor. A camera preview shows the game's setting.

items.title: The levels
items.text:
Level The scene is drawn at What you get Off (default) full size The image as before: sharp, but edges look jagged. Anti-aliasing only (100%) full size Smooth edges, the best image. Costs a little more than Off. Quality (67%) 67% of the width Almost as sharp, a little faster on a modest card. Balanced (58%) 58% In between. Performance (50%) 50% (a quarter of the pixels) Faster, a little softer when the camera moves. Ultra performance (33%) 33% The fastest; blurry when the camera moves. For a very weak card or a very large screen.

What we measured, at 1920 x 1080, on the integrated graphics of an AMD processor: on a continent with its sea, 5.4 ms per frame without upscaling, 4.3 ms with Performance and 3.7 ms with Ultra performance; on a small village the gain is smaller (the scene costs little), and Quality is a little slower than Off there. On a powerful graphics card the difference doesn't show: the image is already very fast.

items.title: Good to know
items.text:
• When the camera stops, the image gets sharper for about a second: that is upscaling blending the frames. In the editor, the view keeps drawing during that time, then rests.
  • A screenshot taken by the agent is always taken at full size, without upscaling. A game capture (--capture) keeps its upscaling, with its method, and its anti-aliasing: the picture is redrawn there until its whole jitter is blended.

items.title: The player chooses too
items.text: With the Menu system, the game's Options button has a Graphics section: the player chooses the quality there (Low, Medium, High or Ultra: see quality), the upscaling (the same levels as above), the anti-aliasing when upscaling is off (see anti-aliasing), the shadows (As quality at first, then High, Medium, Low or Off, for the sun and every light: see light and shadows) and the upscaling method (None, FSR, and DLSS if you provided it; the line only shows when FSR or DLSS works on their card). At first, they find what you set here (and the quality chosen for their machine); each click moves to the next choice, at once. Their choice is kept from one game to the next; your game settings do not change.

items.title: Anti-aliasing
items.text:
When upscaling is off, anti-aliasing smooths the objects' edges, which otherwise look like stairs. (Upscaling, even "Anti-aliasing only", already does it: the choice then no longer matters.)

  • For the game: nothing selected, Game window section, Anti-aliasing. The agent can change it too, and the player chooses it in the game's menu (Display tab).
  • For the editor's views: Preferences, Display, View anti-aliasing (None at first). A camera preview shows the game's.
Choice What it does Automatic (as quality) The game's starting setting: TAA in High and Medium quality, FXAA in Low (TAA would cost 4 ms there on an integrated chip). A project created before 11 November 2026 keeps SMAA in High and Medium: its picture does not change. TAA (sharp in motion) Blends the frames that follow one another, like "Anti-aliasing only": the finest, but each picture is rebuilt from the previous ones. SMAA (sharp, no trails) Recognizes the shape of each edge in the finished picture and smooths it: sharp, nothing trails behind what moves. In High, it finds edges by color; otherwise by brightness. FXAA (lightest) A single pass over the finished picture: the cheapest, a little softer. FSR 2 native (fine lines) AMD's FSR 2 at full size, with its reactive mask (water, glass and particles leave no trail): sharper than SMAA on thin lines, signs and railings, less good on foliage. A choice, never Automatic's; WorldMint's TAA replaces it where FSR does not run. FSR sharpness (0 to 1, 0 by default) sharpens it. None The edges as they are.

What we measured, at 1920 x 1080, on a scene of 225 cubes (graphics card time on top of None):

RTX 5090 AMD Radeon integrated chip FXAA + 0.01 ms + 0.85 ms SMAA + 0.03 ms + 1.5 ms TAA + 0.04 ms + 4.0 ms

Why TAA at first: on dense foliage, it shimmers a third less than SMAA (measured, see ADR-032). Its drawbacks: a slight trail behind what moves fast, a slightly softer picture. To get SMAA back, choose it in Anti-aliasing.

SMAA comes from its authors (Jorge Jimenez et al., MIT license); FXAA is written by WorldMint after the FXAA 3.11 algorithm.

items.title: AMD FSR
items.text:
AMD FSR 2 (FidelityFX Super Resolution 2.2, MIT license) rebuilds the full-size picture from the reduced one, its depth and the motion of each point. It is sharper than WorldMint's method when the picture is much reduced (Performance, Ultra performance), and it works on every graphics card: NVIDIA, AMD or Intel. It is already in WorldMint: nothing to download or provide, and nothing to show in your game.

  • Choosing it: Upscaling method: FSR (all cards). Upscaling switches to Quality if it was off. With Anti-aliasing only (100%), it smooths edges without shrinking the picture.
  • Good to know: when the camera turns fast, in Performance, the grain of soft shadows may show for a moment (WorldMint's method smooths it more, by being blurrier).

What we measured, at 1920 x 1080, on a scene of grass, trees and banners (the graphics card's time for the view, on 11 November 2026):

RTX 5090 AMD Radeon integrated chip (2 cores) Off (full size, no anti-aliasing) 0.64 ms 7.4 ms WorldMint, Anti-aliasing only (100%) 0.40 ms 11.7 ms WorldMint, Quality 0.26 ms 9.0 ms FSR, Anti-aliasing only (100%) 0.53 ms 23.4 ms FSR, Quality 0.36 ms 16.4 ms FSR, Balanced 0.32 ms 14.9 ms FSR, Performance 0.29 ms 14.2 ms

On the RTX 5090, FSR costs 0.1 ms more than WorldMint's method at the same level. (Off costs more than the others there: without upscaling, ray-traced shadows cast several rays per point.) On the small integrated chip of a desktop processor, it costs 5 to 12 ms more: WorldMint's method stays the fastest there; Performance saves 9 ms over Anti-aliasing only.

items.title: NVIDIA DLSS
items.text:
On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX card, upscaling can go through NVIDIA DLSS, sharper than WorldMint's when the image is much smaller. On every other card, the game keeps WorldMint's, without telling the player anything.

WorldMint doesn't provide DLSS. It is NVIDIA software: you download it yourself from NVIDIA, and you are the one who distributes it with your game, under NVIDIA's license. For every game that uses it, even a free one, it asks:

  • NVIDIA's logo when the game starts and in its credits;
  • every use of this logo submitted to NVIDIA, which must approve it in writing, two weeks ahead;
  • to tell NVIDIA before a commercial release of the game.

items.title: Turning it on
items.text:
1. Download Streamline from NVIDIA (Streamline releases) and unzip it. Its files are in bin\x64.
  2. Nothing selected, Game window section: Upscaling method, DLSS (NVIDIA). A window says what the license asks; read it (Read NVIDIA's license), then check I have read it: I will take the steps with NVIDIA myself.
  3. Choose the folder: Streamline's bin\x64 folder. WorldMint checks that sl.interposer.dll, sl.common.dll, sl.dlss.dll and nvngx_dlss.dll are there and carry NVIDIA's digital signature. A missing, changed or otherwise-signed file is refused, with a message.
  4. Turn DLSS on. Upscaling switches to Quality if it was off: the chosen level applies to DLSS too.

For the editor's view: Preferences, Display, View upscaling method, DLSS (NVIDIA), from the next start of the editor.

items.title: In the exported game
items.text:
The export copies NVIDIA's files into the game (nvidia folder, next to the program) only if DLSS is on, and reminds you of the logo and the steps. If they are missing, the game is exported anyway, with WorldMint's upscaling. The agent knows this setting but never turns it on: the agreement with NVIDIA is yours.

What we measured on an RTX 5090, at 1920 x 1080: about 0.4 ms more per frame than WorldMint's upscaling; the game takes about 3 seconds longer to start, while DLSS gets ready.

items.title: Ray tracing
items.text: Usually, a shadow is made by redrawing the scene as seen from the sun, several times per frame (the "shadow maps"): up close it is sharp, but it softens and loses detail further away. Ray tracing works differently: it casts real rays of light through a copy of the scene arranged to be searched quickly. Each point of the picture asks the sun whether it can see it; if an object is in the way, the point is in shadow. The shadow is accurate at every distance, and it can be soft like that of a real sun. The same rays make reflections: water, metal, glass and smooth floors reflect the scenery, even what is off screen.

items.title: Which cards have it
items.text: NVIDIA RTX cards (20 series and later), AMD Radeon RX 6000 and later, and Intel Arc. Some graphics chips built into the processor have it too, but they are too slow to use it in a game (see the measurements below). On every other card, nothing changes: the game is drawn with shadow maps, as before.

items.title: What each quality does
items.text:
Quality With ray tracing Low Never in Automatic: shadow maps, as before. The player can force it (On): it then takes Medium's settings, with a warning. Medium The sun's shadow by a ray, up to 1 km around the camera. Placed lights keep their shadow maps. Ray-traced reflections on what is nearly smooth (roughness up to 0.3: water, polished metal, glass), up to 500 m. High The sun's shadow up to 1.5 km, and the shadow of every placed light that casts one, by one ray each (with no limit on their number). Reflections up to a roughness of 0.5 (blurrier and blurrier), up to 1 km. Indirect lighting (which can be turned off on its own).

Shadow softness (in "Sky and light" for the sun, each light's own softness) applies to rays too: it is the size of what gives the light. With temporal anti-aliasing (the one of upscaling), one ray per point aims at a slightly different spot of the sun at every frame, and the frames are blended; without it, a few rays per point (4 in Medium, 8 in High). The rays' sun is never smaller than the real one (0.5°): a ray-traced shadow never has a perfectly sharp edge. At a softness of 0°, the edge also keeps the blur of the shadow maps: turning ray tracing on does not change the look of shadows, it makes them more accurate (at the foot of objects, far away). Shadows turned Off (the Shadows line of the player's menu, or the scene's shadow quality) turn the rays off too.

items.title: What keeps its shadow maps
items.text:
Rays see a copy of the scene arranged in advance. What is missing from it keeps its shadow through shadow maps, next to the rays:

  • animated characters (their pose changes at every frame; a later step will put them in the copy);
  • objects whose creator shader cuts holes in their surface or moves their vertices (a ray would see the model whole and still).

Particles and water receive the rays' shadows, but do not cast any. A piece of terrain or a tile that has just arrived is arranged within a few frames: meanwhile, it casts no shadow (far away, it does not show).

items.title: Reflections
items.text:
A ray leaves each point of water, metal, glass or a smooth floor, in the direction of the reflection. What it hits is lit as it would be on screen, more simply: its colour, the sun and its shadow, the sky. What reflects this way depends on the material's roughness (see materials): up to 0.3 in Medium, up to 0.5 in High. The rougher a surface, the blurrier its reflection; with temporal anti-aliasing, the ray aims in a slightly different direction at every frame, and the frames are blended. Beyond that roughness, or when the ray hits nothing, the reflection stays as before: the sky.

  • Realistic water keeps the screen's reflections first (they also show characters and all the light); the ray fills in what the screen cannot see, like the shore behind the camera.
  • Stylised water reflects the scenery in each facet, like so many small flat mirrors, slightly blurred and mixed with the sky: it keeps its flat colours.
  • Not reflected by the rays: animated characters, objects whose creator shader cuts holes in or moves their surface, particles, and the light of placed lights on what is reflected (at night, a reflection only shows what glows by itself).

Ambient occlusion (the soft shadow in corners) also uses rays, in Medium and High. Indirect lighting uses rays in Medium and High quality: the light bounced by surfaces (a sunlit floor lights the walls, a room is lit through its window), ray traced with a light cache. In Medium, it is computed at half resolution (one ray for four pixels, gathered afterwards); in High, one ray per pixel, about 1 to 2 ms per frame. On at first, it can be turned off on its own (see below), and Automatic removes it if the card pays too much for it. Off, or in Low, shade gets the sky's ambient light, as before.

items.title: Automatic, On, Off
items.text:
• Automatic (at first): ray tracing only on a dedicated graphics card that has it, in Medium or High quality. Never on an integrated chip, never in Low.
  • On: always, on a card that has it, even where it is heavy (an integrated chip, Low quality). The player's menu then warns them: "Heavy on this card: the picture may slow down". There, only shadows use rays: reflections would cost too much (on an integrated chip, water went from 53 to 97 ms per frame).
  • Off: never; shadow maps, as before.

items.title: Where to set it
items.text:
• For the game: nothing selected, Game window section, Allow ray tracing (ticked by default). Unticked, the game is always drawn without it, on every machine, and the player has no choice. The agent only changes it if you ask.
  • For the player: with the Menu system, Options, Graphics, Ray tracing. The line only appears if their card has it and the game allows it; each click moves from Automatic to On then to Off. Their choice is kept from one play to the next.
  • For the editor's views: Preferences, Display section, View ray tracing (Automatic at first). It only applies to you; the views only use it if the game allows it. A camera's preview shows the game's, in Automatic.
  • Indirect lighting: for the player, the Indirect lighting line under Ray tracing in the menu (On at first, a click moves to Off, kept from one play to the next; a short line says what it does); for the editor's views, Preferences, View indirect lighting (on at first). It works in Medium and High quality, with ray tracing on. A script reads and changes it with game.graphics and game.set_graphics (indirect_light).

items.title: When the graphics card's memory is full
items.text:
Ray tracing keeps a copy of the scene in the graphics card's memory. The game gives itself a share of that memory (most of it on a dedicated card, half on an integrated chip, which shares the PC's memory), and ray tracing never takes more than a quarter of it, nor the room of models and images. When it is full, ray tracing stops arranging anything new, gives back what is used least, then reaches less far; as a last resort it turns itself off: shadows come back from shadow maps at the next frame, without a stutter. The player's menu says so under the Ray tracing line ("Off: the graphics card's memory is full (classic shadows)"), and so do the editor's Preferences. It tries again as soon as the choice or the quality changes.

Large model images that have not been shown for a few seconds may also drop to a small resolution meanwhile: they stay visible, a little blurry, and become sharp again by themselves when they are seen again and there is room again.

items.title: What we measured
items.text:
On the city of the large-worlds bench (4 × 4 km with its countryside), at 1920 × 1080, High quality, on 10 November 2026:

  • on an NVIDIA RTX 5090, the card's time to draw a view stays the same: 0.17 ms in the street (shadow maps or rays), 0.15 against 0.18 ms flying over (where rays give the whole city its shadow, shadow maps only the first 150 metres); in the full city (100 % step), 0.39 ms with rays against 0.50 ms with shadow maps, and the whole frame goes from 4.4 to 3.2 ms. The scene arranged for rays takes 200 to 240 MB of the card (compacting gives back 440); everything is arranged in a little over 2 seconds at start-up, with no hitch over 3 ms;
  • on the integrated graphics chip of an AMD processor (forced On), the same view costs 9 to 10 ms more per frame (21 to 23 ms instead of 11 to 14), and the scene takes 260 to 600 MB of the PC's memory: too heavy for a smooth game. That is why Automatic never turns it on there;
  • reflections (on 10 November, on an island by the sea with polished metal, a mirror and a pane of glass) cost 0.05 to 0.1 ms per frame on the RTX 5090; in a city with nothing smooth, nothing. On the integrated chip they almost doubled the frame time (53 → 95 ms): where ray tracing is forced and heavy, they stay off;
  • when objects move (doors, physics), the scene arranged for rays is updated instead of rebuilt: in the full city, its preparation goes from 6 ms to 0.14 ms per frame.
  • what arrives (a tile, a model) is arranged for the rays in 2 ms at most per frame (1.5 in Medium), at the card's measured pace: on the integrated chip forced On, crossing the city went from 376 to 53 frames over 16.7 ms.

items.title: Particles and decals
items.text:
Particles bring the world to life: a campfire, a torch, smoke, sparks, magic, rain or snow, and what goes with an action (wood chips when chopping a tree, dust when the player lands, a flash when a hit lands). Decals lay an image on the ground or a wall: a footprint, an impact, a scorch mark, a stain, a puddle, a sign.

Everything is set without code. The effects are generic: they depend on no model, and chips take the colour of what is hit, measured on the model itself.

items.title: An effect on an object
items.text:
The Particle effect system goes on the object the effect comes from: a campfire, a torch, a cauldron. For an effect on its own (a fire in the middle of a camp, snow over a valley), Create > Particle effect places an invisible box that carries it: its settings come first in its properties, before its place and size. The effect already runs in the editor's view while you set it.

Its settings, in the object's properties:

  • Effect: fire (dancing flames, a brighter core, a warm glow, embers flying up and a little smoke), smoke, sparks, magic, rain, snow, dust, chips, explosion, hit impact.
  • Size: 1 for a campfire, 0.4 for a torch, 3 for a big blaze. For rain and snow, the width of the area where they fall.
  • Colour: the effect's own, or a chosen colour (a blue fire, green magic).
  • Amount: the number of particles, multiplied.
  • Looping: ticked, the effect runs as long as the object is there; unticked, it plays once when the game starts.
  • Duration and Height above the object's base (the flame at the tip of a torch).
  • Effect light and Light strength (fire, explosion, magic, sparks, hit): the light the effect gives around it, with its shadows, without them, or none (see the light of fires and effects).

Placed on a visible object, the effect stops while the object is hidden and comes back when it is shown. Place rain or snow on the player: it follows them everywhere.

items.title: Playing an effect with the Trigger
items.text:
The Trigger has two actions:

  • Play an effect: on the target, the one it carries (its Particle effect system, lit again: a brazier lit by a lever), or a ready-made effect played once (an explosion, chips, magic), with its size.
  • Stop an effect: puts out the effect the target carries.

For example, a barrel that explodes when broken: When: It dies, Then: Play an effect, Explosion, size 2; then a rule that destroys it.

items.title: What the game already does
items.text:
• The player raises a little dust when landing after a jump or a fall (Player tab, Dust on landing, to turn it off).
  • An object that bursts or collapses makes chips in its colour and dust; an object that falls raises dust where it hits the ground.
  • Gathering sends chips flying at each hit, from the spot hit and in its colour (wood for a tree's trunk, stone for a rock): setting Chips at each hit.
  • Simple combat makes a flash, sparks and a little dust when a hit lands: setting A flash and sparks when a hit lands.

items.title: A decal
items.text:
Create > Decal places a flat invisible box that carries the Decal system. Its image covers the box's width and depth, and lies on what is around its base: the ground, a floor, a rock. The box's scale sets the image's size; turning it around its height turns the image. Its settings come first in its properties.

  • Image: a stain, an impact, a scorch mark, a puddle, footprints, a skid mark (drawn by the engine), or an image of the project (PNG or JPEG, its transparency kept).
  • Opacity: from 0 (invisible) to 1.
  • Tint: white leaves the image as it is; dark red makes a blood stain, green a puddle of poison.

For a sign on a wall, tip the box so that its height points out of the wall, and place its base against it. The image lies on everything inside the box, characters included: keep it thin where people walk.

items.title: With a script
items.text:
The agent can also write a script:

  • game.effect("explosion", position, {size = 2}) plays an effect at a place; game.effect("eclats", rock) on an object (its chips take its colour). With loop = true, the effect runs until game.stop_effect.
  • game.object_effect(fire, false) puts out the effect an object carries, true lights it again.
  • game.decal("impact", position, {size = 1.5}) places a decal; life = 10 fades it out after ten seconds.

The details are in the script reference.

items.title: Light on effects
items.text: Smoke, dust, chips, rain, snow and decals are lit like the rest of the scene: by the sun, darker in the shadow of a roof or a tree, and by the placed lights close by (smoke passing in front of a lantern takes its colour). Fire, sparks, magic, explosions and hit impacts make their own light: they stay just as bright at night, and light up what is around them, with shadows for fire, explosions and magic: a cube next to a campfire casts its shadow. Nothing to place next to them; the details are in the light of fires and effects.

items.title: The agent's test
items.text: Particles are simulated by the game itself: the same game gives exactly the same particles. When the agent tests the game, its report counts the effects played by name, the particles born and the most alive at once, and the decals placed; its captures show them.

items.title: In the editor's view
items.text: An effect that can be seen in a view animates on its own, even when you touch nothing (30 frames per second in the view you are working in, 10 in the others): you see the fire dance while you adjust it. When no effect can be seen any more (out of view, or put out), the editor goes back to rest, and so does the graphics card.

items.title: Effect quality levels
items.text:
Effects follow the graphics quality, on three levels:

High Medium Low Particles at once, at most 6,000 3,000 1,500 Particles given off all three quarters, a little larger half, a little larger Light on smoke and dust the sun and its shadows, placed lights and their shadows without the placed lights' shadows the sun and the sky, no shadow Largest size of a particle on screen 90% of the image height 70% 50% Decals placed by the game, at once 128 96 48

An effect never breaks the game: beyond their number, new particles are not born, it only looks lighter. The same goes for decals placed during the game: beyond their limit, the oldest fades out to make room for the new one. The game started with --low-power takes Low; --particles low, medium or high chooses the effects' level on its own.

A particle brushing past the camera fades out instead of covering the whole screen, and none goes beyond its largest size on screen: walking through smoke does not slow the game down.

items.title: Exporting a game
items.text: Exporting turns your game into a standalone folder, with its .exe program, that anyone can run on Windows, without WorldMint. Like WorldMint, the game needs a graphics card that supports Vulkan 1.3, with an up-to-date driver: otherwise, it tells the player as soon as it opens.

items.title: Exporting
items.text:
1. Check that the game has a player (Set as player on a character): without a player, Export game... is greyed out.
  2. Give the game a title: in the game's settings (nothing selected), Game window section, Title field ("Jeu" at first). The folder and the program take this name; without a title, the project's.
  3. File > Export game..., then choose the folder to put it in.

The status bar shows "Exporting the game...", then "Game exported: ... (15 MB)", and the folder opens in File Explorer. The editor stays usable during the export.

The agent can also export the game for you.

items.title: What the folder contains
items.text:
My game/
  My game.exe       the game
  locales/          its texts, in French and English
  data/             its scenes, and only the models, animations, sounds and images it really uses

All the project's scenes go with the game, as they are saved (the open scene, as it is on screen). The exported game starts on the project's start scene, whichever one you were looking at.

items.title: The checks
items.text:
• Before replacing anything, the editor runs the exported game, without a window, to check that it starts. If it does not start, the export is refused ("The exported game does not start: ...") and the previous export stays intact.
  • An export replaces the previous one in the same folder. A folder with the same name that is not an export is never overwritten ("This folder exists and is not an export"). If the exported game is still open, close it first.
  • Warnings (a file named by a script but missing, a path specific to your computer...) show in the console, starting with "Export warning", with the script's name and line.
  • A path built in pieces in a script (PACK .. "JPG/Panel.jpg") cannot be read whole by the export: it looks in the project and the library for the one file whose path ends with the written piece, and puts it in the game at the same place as in the project, where the script will look for it. If several files end the same way, or none, a warning says so: write the whole path in the script.

Players' saved games (game.save in a script) are kept between two plays of the exported game.

items.title: The game's log
items.text: The exported game writes what happens to it (network connections, script errors, warnings) in a log, next to the player's saves: %APPDATA%\WorldMint\<game name>\journal.txt (type this path in the Windows Explorer address bar). The previous play is kept in journal.1.txt. The log never goes beyond 2 MB per file and never contains a password or a player key. When a tester has a problem, especially in a game with several players over the Internet, ask them for these two files.

items.title: Publishing an update
items.text:
You fixed a bug, added a level: here is how to give the new version to your players.

  1. Change the game's version: game settings (nothing selected), Publication section, Game version field ("1.0" for a new game). Digits and dots: 1.0, 1.0.1, 1.1… The Raise the version button moves to the next one (1.0.3 becomes 1.0.4). Players see it in small print at the bottom right of the title screen (Menu system), and the game's log writes it at start ("jeu : Harvest rush 1.0.4"). A script reads it with game.version().
  2. Export again: File > Export the game..., into the same folder. The new folder replaces the old one. With Also make a .zip file (Publication section, on by default), the export also writes <title>-<version>.zip next to the folder ("Harvest rush-1.0.4.zip"): the same folder, in a single file, ready to send. Files are stored as they are, without compression. Nothing is sent anywhere: you put it online yourself.
  3. Put it online, depending on where your players find the game:
    • itch.io: on your game's page, Edit game, then upload the new .zip file (and remove the old one). Or, with butler, itch.io's tool, in one line: butler push "Harvest rush" myaccount/harvest-rush:windows --userversion 1.0.4. butler only sends what changed, and players who installed the game with the itch app get the update by themselves.
    • Steam: you need a Steamworks account (Steam's developer account) and a page for the game, which costs a fee to open. The exported folder is the content of one "depot" of your game. You upload it with SteamPipe, either with the command-line tool steamcmd or with ContentBuilder (in the Steamworks kit), following the Steamworks documentation; then, on the Steamworks site, you publish that new "build" on a branch (the default branch for everyone). Steam then updates every player.
    • GOG, Epic Games Store, or your own website: send the .zip file with the store's tool, or offer it for download on your site.

Good to know:

  • Players' saves do not move: they are in %APPDATA%\WorldMint\<game name>, not in the game's folder. Keep the same game title, or the game looks for its saves elsewhere.
  • Renaming or deleting objects of the world can upset an old save: what it said about those objects no longer finds its place. Adding is safe.
  • With several players, everyone needs the same version. A player with another version cannot join the game, and the game tells them why: "The host has version 1.0.4, you have 1.0.3: update your game" (or, if the host is behind, that the host needs to update their game).

items.title: Writing an extension
items.text:
An extension adds a complete tool to WorldMint without touching the engine: the city generator is the first one. It lives in its own folder, extensions/<id>/, and only uses what the engine offers it. The engine itself knows no extension.

This page is for people who write WorldMint's code. To use an extension, there is nothing to do: it shows up in the editor by itself.

items.title: An extension's folder
items.text:
extensions/<id>/
  extension.json      its identity
  <id>_extension.cpp  the file that registers it at startup
  moteur/ editeur/ agent/ contenu/ essais/   (depending on what it does)

extension.json says what it is:

{ "id": "ville", "name": "Ville", "version": "0.1.0", "minEditorVersion": "0.4.0", "paid": true }
  • id: the name of its folder and of its place in the scene; lowercase letters, digits, _ and -.
  • minEditorVersion: the oldest WorldMint version it works with. An older version refuses it and says which version is needed.
  • paid: true for a paid extension.

items.title: Building it
items.text:
In CMakeLists.txt, an option turns it on, and worldmint_extension(<id> <sources>...) adds its sources to the editor and to the tests:

option(WORLDMINT_EXTENSION_VILLE "Builds the Ville extension" ON)
if(WORLDMINT_EXTENSION_VILLE)
    worldmint_extension(ville extensions/ville/ville_extension.cpp)
endif()

Its extension.json is copied into the program: the file that registers it reads it through kExtensionManifest (#include "extensions/<id>/extension_manifest.h").

items.title: Registering it
items.text:
At startup, the extension introduces itself to the registry, with what it brings:

engine::ExtensionRegistry::instance().add(info, editorTools, agentTools, derivedTiles);
  • An editor tool (EditorToolHook): a section, placed with the world settings (where the terrain lives), when nothing is selected. It receives the scene, the history (every change goes through a command that Ctrl+Z undoes), the project folder and the view. Its title is translated like the rest of the editor.
  • If it works in the view (viewport), it also has its button in the tool bar, under the terrain tools (tooltip). Picked, it receives the clicks of the view and its options bar opens at the bottom of the view (options). It draws over every view, picked or not.
  • Its long work runs in the background (frame, every frame): it says so in the fixed status line (status), and asks the editor to read its derived objects again when their cache changed (derivedChanged). The editor never freezes.
  • A tool built only in the editor (it draws with ImGui) is added from its own file, with addEditorTool(id, tool).
  • Agent tools (AgentToolHook): a name prefixed by the extension, an English description, the schema of their arguments. They join the agent's tool list.
  • Agent guides: extensions/<id>/agent/guides.json (in the format of agent/guides.json: the guides, their "when" line, the guide of each tool) and one .md file per guide. They are copied into the program (extension_guides.h) and join the agent's guides when the extension is allowed. tools/check_agent_guides.py checks them, like the others.
  • Derived objects (DerivedTileHook): what the extension produces for one tile of the world.

items.title: Its data in the scene
items.text:
Each extension has its place in the scene file, under its id:

"extensions": { "ville": { ... } }

It reads and writes whatever it wants there. This place is read and written back unchanged, even when the scene is opened without the extension: nothing is lost.

items.title: Derived objects
items.text:
What an extension produces (the streets of a city, for example) is not saved in the scene. For each tile, it is stored in the project cache, <project>/.worldmint/<id>/<tile>/: its files, and objects.json, the list of objects. On load, these objects are read back from the cache and carry generatedBy: a game without the extension still shows them.

They can be looked at and selected, but not changed, moved or deleted, neither in the editor nor by the agent: they never enter the history. The properties say which extension produced them. To change them, change the extension's data, with its tool.

The export takes this cache along into data/.worldmint/<id>/ (never .worldmint/cache/): the exported game reads the derived objects back on load, without the extension. A scene only receives the objects of the extensions that have data in it.

items.title: The licence
items.text: A single function decides whether an extension is open: extensionAllowed(id). Today, it is open as soon as it is built and accepts this WorldMint version. Later, it will also read the WorldMint account's licence. An extension that is not open adds nothing: no tool, no derived object; its data stays kept in the scene. The editor says so once at startup, in its log, with the reason (a WorldMint version that is too old, a missing licence).

items.title: Tests
items.text:
An extension's tests go in extensions/<id>/essais/ and run with WorldMint's own, for every version. The hooks themselves are tested in tests/test_extensions.cpp.

They are added to engine_tests only, next to worldmint_extension(...):

target_sources(engine_tests PRIVATE extensions/ville/essais/test_city_plan.cpp)

items.title: The City example
items.text:
The “Cities and roads” extension (its id stays ville) keeps its plan (street profiles, nodes, segments) in its place in the scene, and changes it only through an undoable command. Its derived-object hook produces, for each tile its streets touch:

  • chaussee.glb: the roadway, the sidewalks with their curbs, the road markings;
  • empreinte.txt: the fingerprint of what the tile draws. A tile whose fingerprint has not changed is not rewritten: moving a point only rebuilds the tiles it touches. It includes the city computation version (ville- and 12 characters), the fingerprint of the city engine's sources and of the data it reads, computed at build time: a new WorldMint version that changes the generation rebuilds every tile by itself;
  • one derived object, ville/<tile>/chaussee, which shows that model.

The .glb format is glTF 2.0: the engine writes it itself (assets/glb_writer.h) and reads it back like any other model.

Its editor tool, City (Streets and Districts modes, plan view, "Generate a city…": see The city), only changes the plan, through that command: each gesture is one step. Its frame hook rebuilds the cache on a thread, from a copy of the scene, and says "Updating the city…" or "Generating the city…" meanwhile: the editor never freezes. The plan view uses frameFromAbove.

Its agent tools do the same, one undoable step per call, with refusals in English:

Tool What it does city_generate A whole city (center, size or area, seed, districts; replace to replace the existing city); or a town in a zone (outline, or center, size and angle), with ambiance and name, next to the others. city_town_set A named town (town): rename it (name), lay it out again (regenerate, seed), delete it (delete). city_road_add A street between two points or two nodes (from, to, via), with its profile and name. city_road_set The profile, name, path or crossing of a street (a refused bridge), its deletion; a node (roundabout, position). city_get The plan in less than 3,000 characters, by pages: streets, nodes, districts, styles. city_check Crossings without a junction, slopes too steep, segments too short, unwanted dead ends, orphan overrides, parcels without access. city_district_set Add a district, change its style, name or outline, another draw, delete it. city_style_set A district style or a street profile: create it from another one, set its values, delete it.

Its guides, city and city-districts (extensions/ville/agent/), tell them to work at the level of the plan and to check with a picture. Its starting data (the seven district styles, the lists of street names) is in extensions/ville/contenu/, copied into the program at build time.

items.title: What the free engine keeps
items.text:
The City is a paid extension ("paid": true). The engine stays free and holds nothing specific to the city. The hooks it uses are generic, and serve any extension:

  • the registry and the licence (extensionAllowed), the editor tool (section, palette button, options bar, view clicks, background work, status line), the agent's tools and guides;
  • the place in the scene, read and written back intact without the extension;
  • derived objects and their cache, taken along by the export and read back without the extension: a game made with the city plays everywhere. A derived object can name a model of the project's library (DerivedObject::asset) and say it lies on the ground (groundCover): its simplified versions seen from afar do not go under the ground;
  • plant-free areas of the terrain (Terrain::clearings): the terrain's sowing avoids the areas an extension gives it (the roadway, the sidewalks), and the plants come back when the area goes;
  • the framed top view (frameFromAbove);
  • an extension's content as data (contenu/*.json), copied into the program by worldmint_extension.

items.title: The editor
items.text:
I made a mistake. How do I go back? Ctrl+Z, as many times as needed; Ctrl+Y redoes. This also applies to what the agent did. Under each answer of the agent, Undo these changes undoes its whole turn at once.

The editor closed before I saved. Have I lost everything? No. An automatic backup keeps a copy of your work every 60 seconds. On the next launch, the editor offers Recover your work?: click Recover, then save (Ctrl+S).

Where are my files? In the project folder: File > Open project folder. The first project is in Documents\WorldMint\Mon premier jeu. See Projects and scenes.

An object disappeared from the view. It may be hidden by the eye of the scene list: View > Show everything again. Or it is elsewhere: select it in the list, then F to frame the view on it.

My model does not appear in the library. The editor reads .glb, .gltf, .fbx and .obj files. COLLADA files (.dae) are counted as "Not read (COLLADA)". Also check that its folder was added (Add a folder).

My model is tiny or gigantic. Change its Scale in the properties. The sizes that trigger a warning are set in the game's settings, Technical settings section.

How do I switch the editor to French? Help > Language > Français, or the Preferences.

The text is too small. Preferences > Interface size.

items.title: The game
items.text:
The Play button does nothing. The game needs a player: the console says "No player: select an object, then choose "Set as player"." Select a character and click Set as player.

The player falls through the ground. The ground needs a Collision (Appearance section of its properties), or must be a terrain.

The player appears anywhere when arriving in a scene. The scene has no arrival point, or the passage does not name one: see Linking scenes.

How do I get the mouse out of the game window? Esc frees it (unless the game uses Esc for its own pause).

The game crashed. The editor and your scene are safe: the console says "The game crashed (code ...)". Start again with F5.

How do I change the look of my game's menu or inventory? In the list of screens (Interface panel), open the screen under its system's name, then format its shapes with the ribbon and the Format pane: see Change the look of a system's window. Back to the system's version puts the original screen back.

Why can't I delete a button of a window? It carries the Required badge: its system needs it. You can format it, move it or hide it, but not delete it. Optional shapes can be deleted.

My game has a city: does it work without the Cities and roads extension? Yes. The roadway is stored in the project and goes with the export: the exported game shows the city without the extension. See The city.

How do I change the game's keys? Game controls panel, in Developer mode: see Game controls.

How do I give my game to someone? File > Export game...: see Exporting a game. Send the whole exported folder.

items.title: The agent
items.text:
Do I have to pay to use the agent? The agent works with your own account: a Claude subscription (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise), a usage-billed account (Anthropic Console, API key), or for Codex a ChatGPT account or an OpenAI API key. That account counts the agent's usage, under its own terms; under each answer, the editor shows the cost when the account is billed by usage.

Can the agent touch my files or my computer? No. It only has the editor's tools, which act on the open project: see What the agent does. An agent that arrives with other tools is stopped before it does anything.

The agent no longer answers. The panel says so after a while without news. It may still be working; the square button stops it. You can then write to it again: the conversation goes on.

Can it see what I see? It can look at the scene as an image by itself. You can also attach A capture of the 3D view, an image or a PDF (paperclip of the input area).

Can it use my models? Yes, all those in the library. If a folder is not there yet, write its path in your message: it is added.

How do I change the way it works? Agent settings > Agent rules > Customize for this project creates an AGENT.md file in the project, which you can edit. Or simply tell it: your request comes before its rules.

Which model should I choose? Default is fine. A higher reasoning effort gives more thought-out answers, but slower ones.

items.title: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields
items.text:
Everything your game shows on top of the scene (a title screen, a pause, a shop, a dialogue box, an inventory, a health bar, a chat window) is the game interface. It is made of screens. Each screen is formatted with the mouse in the screen editor, like a PowerPoint slide: shapes, with a background, an outline, a shadow, an icon and a text.

There are two kinds of screens:

  • the screens delivered by the systems: the Menu brings its title screen and its pause, the Inventory its window and its quick bar, the Health bar its bar… You change their look, add buttons to them, remove what you don't want: the system keeps filling them and reacting to clicks;
  • your own screens: a score, a timer, a help panel, a workshop menu. You draw them yourself, or the agent draws them for you.

The look shared by the whole game (colors, text size, corners, images of an interface pack) is set in one place, with the Interface system.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: What the interface can show
items.text:
A screen is made of shapes. Each shape has a kind:

Kind What it is Shape A rectangle, a rounded rectangle, a circle, a pill, a diamond, a triangle or a star, which can carry an icon and a text, and contain other shapes. Text A text, which wraps by itself within the given width. It can have words in bold and words in color. Button A shape you click: it opens or closes a screen, sends an event, or runs an action of the system. Image and Icon An image of the project (a logo, a portrait), or an icon drawn by WorldMint (a heart, a drop, a star, a sword…). Gauge A bar that fills up: health, stamina, progress. Field A box where the player types text: their name, a message, a code. Panel A background that arranges what it contains: in a column, in a row or in a grid. Panels nest: a menu in a panel, inventory slots in a grid. List A panel whose first shape is a row template: the game repeats it for each item (the objects of an inventory, the scores). With a given height, it scrolls with the mouse wheel, with a thin scroll bar.

The game places the shapes of a panel itself, one after the other: there are no positions to work out.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: The mouse
items.text: In the game, the cursor is hidden and the mouse turns the camera. When the game opens an interface you click in (an inventory, a menu), it shows the cursor: the camera no longer turns with the mouse, and the Basic combat system no longer strikes. The agent takes care of it when it writes the menu.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Text fields
items.text:
A text field behaves the same way in every game made with WorldMint:

  • A click on the field selects it and puts the cursor there: what the player types is written where the cursor is. Backspace erases the character before the cursor, Delete the one after.
  • The arrows, Home and End move the cursor; with Ctrl, the arrows jump a whole word (and Backspace erases it).
  • Shift with the arrows, or dragging the mouse with the button held, selects text; Ctrl+A selects everything. A letter typed replaces the selection.
  • Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X and Ctrl+V copy, cut and paste, with the Windows clipboard: a name copied elsewhere can be pasted.
  • On a gamepad, once the field is selected: the d-pad moves the cursor, A validates, B leaves the field. Writing needs a keyboard.
  • While a field is selected, the player does not move and no game control fires: typing "w" writes a w, without moving the character.
  • Enter validates the field and leaves it. The game receives the text, and the player can move again.
  • Escape, or a click elsewhere, leaves the field without validating it.

Keeping the field active after Enter

For a chat window, you often want to send several messages in a row, without clicking in the field again. That is not the standard behavior: it takes a script that selects the field again after each message. Ask the agent for it, for example: "In the chat window, after Enter, send the message, empty the field and keep it active."
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Gamepad and keyboard
items.text:
Every window of the game can also be used without a mouse, with nothing to write: the game finds its buttons by itself.

Gamepad Keyboard What it does D-pad or left stick Arrow keys Moves to the next button in that direction, by its place on screen. Held, it keeps moving: you go down a long list without pressing for each line. Tab Moves to the next button, and back to the first after the last. A Enter Clicks the chosen button. B Escape Closes the window, or goes back (from the options to the pause).
  • The chosen button shows from afar: lighter, with a thick frame in the accent color of the Interface system.
  • With a gamepad, a window that opens chooses its first button at once. With a keyboard, the first arrow shows the chosen button, the next one moves it.
  • A list that scrolls follows the chosen button.
  • While choosing in a window, the character does not move, and the buttons used by the window do not fire their control: A does not jump, the d-pad does not drink a potion.
  • The mouse works as before: as soon as it moves, the frame disappears, and the hovered button becomes the chosen one.

The engine does this for every window: the systems' windows as well as those the agent writes. The button that B and Escape click is the one the window marks as its "Close" or "Back" button; a window without one (a dialogue in progress) lets Escape open the pause, as usual.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: The screen editor
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Where to find it
items.text:
• In Developer mode, the Interface panel: the Interface button at the top of the Systems panel, or the Windows menu. Without free panels, it is the Interface screens section of the Game tab. Creator mode does not have the screen editor: ask the agent, or switch to Developer mode.
  • A click on a screen of the list opens it above the 3D view, in the Interface screen tab. The list at the top right shows it at the size of the game window, or in 16/9, 16/10, 4/3, 21/9 and as a phone held upright. The cross closes it.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: The list of screens
items.text:
The screens are arranged in groups, folded with a click:

Group What it holds One group per system (Menu, Round, Inventory…) The screens that system delivered when it was installed. They are formatted like yours; their required shapes cannot be deleted. My game The screens you drew, or the agent drew. A small crossed-out eye says a screen is hidden at start (an announcement, a key or a script shows it). In the world What follows the 3D world: the names above heads, the bubbles, the markers. They do not open here: the systems draw them with the game's styles, so changing a style changes their look.

At the top of the list, New screen creates an empty screen in My game, and The game screen shows everything the player sees at start, together.

A delivered screen you have changed carries the Modified badge. When chosen, it offers Back to the system's version: your changes to that screen are lost, and Ctrl+Z brings them back.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: The open screen
items.text:
From top to bottom, in the middle:

  1. The ribbon, like PowerPoint's (see below).
  2. Shown as in the game, for a system's screen: the preview takes its texts from a short trial of the game, without a window, at the moment the system shows this screen ("The texts come from a trial of the game"). If the screen serves several windows, the list chooses which one. When no trial is possible, the preview shows the test values.
  3. The preview, at the chosen size. A click chooses a shape, drag it to move it, pull its handles to resize it.
  4. The check bar, under the preview: in green, The screen is complete; otherwise, in red, each problem in one sentence ("The required shape "Bouton Jouer" is missing: the system needs it", "This button does nothing", "… opens a screen that does not exist"). A click on a problem chooses its shape.

On the left, under the list, Layers of "…" shows the shapes of the open screen, those a shape contains arranged under it. A click chooses a shape (Ctrl+click adds one), the eye hides or shows it again, the padlock locks it, a right click offers Delete the shape. Each shape of a delivered screen carries a badge:

Badge What it means Required (with a padlock) The system needs it. It can be formatted and moved, but not deleted. Optional Delivered by the system, it can be deleted if you don't want it. Yours You added it to this screen.

Test values. In the Format pane, Test value gives a shape what the preview shows instead of the text the system will write ("3", "Apple x3"); Remove the test value takes it away. The game never uses it: it is only to see the room a text will take.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: The ribbon
items.text:
Tab What it offers Home Undo and Redo; the style gallery, each tile really drawn (a click gives the style to the chosen shape); More, which opens Manage styles; Copy formatting and Paste formatting, like Word's format painter. Insert Shape (a gallery of 7 outlines), Text, Button, Image, Icon, Gauge, Field, Panel, List. The new shape lands in the middle of the screen, or inside the chosen shape if it contains others. Shape (when a shape is chosen) Shape outline, Background, Outline, Shadow, Icon, Icon position; New style from this shape; Back to the style. Text (when the shape has a text) The font, size, bold, italic, underline, color and alignment of the text. Layout Align on the screen (Left, Center, Right, Top, In the middle, Bottom); Bring to front, Move forward, Move back, Send to back; the anchoring; with several shapes chosen, Distribute horizontally, Distribute vertically, Same width, Same height, Same size. Display Zoom out, Zoom in, Fit the screen, and the Magnet (a shape you drag snaps to the edges and centers of the others).

Each tool has a tooltip. When room runs out, the ribbon wraps to a new line instead of hiding tools.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: The Format pane
items.text:
When a shape is chosen, the right panel becomes the Format pane. Its sections fold:

Section What it sets Style The style the shape follows, with "(modified)" if you changed something by hand, or "(not found)" if its style no longer exists. Back to the style forgets the changes made by hand; New style… makes a style from the look of this shape. Shape The shape outline: rectangle, rounded rectangle (with the corner radius), circle, pill, diamond, triangle, star, or None (text only). Background None, Color, Gradient (two colors and a direction), Image (with its images per state and its stretchable frame) or Theme skin (the images of the interface pack, shown as thumbnails). Outline and shadow The color and thickness of the outline; the color, offset and blur of the shadow; the opacity of the shape and of everything it contains. Content The icon or picture (a file of the project, a cell of an icon sheet, or a built-in icon), its position relative to the text, its size and its tint; then the text and its formatting. Behavior On click (see below); and whether the shape is a gauge, a text field, a list, whether it is disabled or hidden at start.

Further down remain the Layout of a panel (column, row, grid), the Value shown in the game, the element's name and Position and size (the anchor to a corner, an edge or the center of the screen, the offset and the size, as a share of the screen).

On click offers:

  • Nothing: the shape does not click;
  • the actions of the screen's system: on the Menu's title screen, "Play", "Options", "Quit"…; on a Round screen, "Start the game";
  • Open the screen…, Close this screen, Replace with the screen…, Open or close the screen…;
  • Send the event…: an event name, answered by a Trigger rule or a script;
  • Trigger action…: a reusable ready-made action of the Trigger.

When nothing is chosen, the right panel shows the screen itself: its name, When to show it (at the start of the game, on announcements, or with a control such as I for an inventory), whether it shows the cursor and whether it pauses the game, the list of its elements, and Delete the screen.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Styles
items.text:
A style is a named look, like Word's styles: "Main button", "Window title", "Inventory slot". All the shapes that follow a style change together when you change it.

  • Create a style: choose a shape formatted the way you like, then New style… (Format pane, Style section) or New style from this shape (ribbon, Shape tab). Give it a name: the shape follows it.
  • Give a style: choose another shape, then click the style in the gallery of the Home tab, or choose it in the Style section.
  • Manage styles (Home › More): each style of the game with the number of shapes that follow it, and buttons to edit it (the style opens in the Format pane, its shapes change live; Done closes it), rename it (its shapes follow), duplicate it and delete it (after confirmation).
  • Delivered styles. A system can deliver its own styles with its screens; their tooltip says so ("Delivered by the system…"). A style can be based on another: it changes only what it gives and follows the rest of the one it starts from.
  • Apply the game theme (in Manage styles) brings into the game the styles of the Interface system's theme (button, panel, text…). Your own styles are kept; if you had changed a style with the same name, the editor warns you before replacing it.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: The theme, and the background you choose
items.text:
A shape with no background of its own takes the look of the theme: the colors of the Interface system, or, if you gave it an interface pack (its image theme setting), the image of its kind (window, button, slot, bar…).

A background you choose always wins: a color, a gradient or an image chosen for a shape (by hand or by a style of the game) shows on every kind of shape (slots, buttons, panels…), even with an image theme. Theme skin gives the shape back to the theme.

One exception: some shapes delivered by a system (Crafting slots, the experience bar…) have a "fallback" background, which only shows without an image theme. The Format pane says so, and the Show this background anyway button shows it as it is.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Shortcuts
items.text: Gesture What it does Click, Ctrl+click Chooses a shape; adds a shape to, or removes it from, the choice. Drag, pull a handle Moves the shape; resizes it. Alt during the gesture: without the magnet. Arrow keys Nudge the chosen shape; with Shift, by a tiny step. Delete Deletes the chosen shape (refused for a required shape: the check bar says why). Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y Undo, redo. A drag or a dragged slider makes only one step.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Step by step
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Change the look of a system's window
items.text:
For example, give round, golden buttons to the title screen:

  1. In the list of screens, open the Menu group and click Écran titre (the title screen).
  2. Click the Play button in the preview (or Bouton Jouer in the layers).
  3. Ribbon, Shape tab: Shape outline › Pill; Background › Gradient, two shades of gold; Outline, 2 pixels.
  4. To give the same look to the other buttons: New style from this shape, name it "Golden button", then choose each other button and click Golden button in the Home gallery. Or: Copy formatting on the first one, Paste formatting on the others.
  5. Look at the check bar: The screen is complete. Run the game (F5): the title screen has its new buttons, and they still do what they did.

The screen now carries the Modified badge. Nothing is lost: Back to the system's version puts it back the way the system delivered it.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Add a button to a window, or remove one
items.text:
Add: open the screen, choose the shape that should receive the button (the window, a column), then Insert › Button. Write its text (Format pane, Content), then say what it does in Behavior › On click: an action of the system ("Quit"), open another screen, send an event for the Trigger, or a ready-made action. The new button carries the Yours badge. As long as it does nothing, the check bar points it out.

Remove: choose the shape and press Delete (or right click in the layers › Delete the shape). An Optional shape disappears, and the system does without it: the Options button of the title screen, for example. A Required shape cannot be deleted; if you don't want to see it, hide it (the eye in the layers), but the check bar will remind you the player will not see it.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Create your own screen
items.text:
1. New screen, at the top of the list: an empty screen opens in My game.
  2. Insert: a Shape for the background (a rounded rectangle), then, with the shape chosen, a Text and a Gauge: they go inside it.
  3. Format it with the ribbon and the Format pane, and give styles to keep the same look everywhere.
  4. What it shows in the game, without code: the Value shown in the game section (see below). A click on The player's health binds a gauge to health.
  5. When to show it: with nothing chosen, the right panel shows the screen. It can be there from the start (a score, a health bar), or wait for an announcement (atelier.ouvrir, which a Trigger sends when the player walks into the workshop) or for a game control that opens and closes it (I). A screen with buttons must show the cursor; a menu can pause the game.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: What a screen shows in the game
items.text:
The Value shown in the game section (for your screens; the systems' screens are filled by their system):

Read from For example A game announcement The player's health, in one click: the sante.change announcement of the Health system, its vie field over its max field. A gauge fills, a text writes "Health: 75 / 100" with the format Health: {valeur} / {max}. A game value A score a script gives with game.set_value("score", 12), shown by "Score: {valeur}". An object's system A value of a system placed on the player or on a named object.

In the editor, a bound value shows an example (75 out of 100), to see the room it will take.

A script can also fill a screen: game.screen_show("atelier") and game.screen_hide("atelier") show and hide it; game.screen_set("atelier/Titre", {text = "Forge"}) changes a shape (its text, its color, whether it is hidden…); game.screen_list("atelier/Recettes", rows) fills a list; game.on_screen_action("fabriquer", fn) answers a button. A shape that no longer exists (an optional shape you deleted) is ignored without an error. See the scripts reference.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: An interface pack: frames, buttons and bars as images
items.text:
