An interface pack (frames, buttons, bars, icon sheets as PNG) is used as it is, without assuming anything about its sizes or names: the editor measures each image.

  • For the whole game: give an image to each kind of element in the image theme setting of the Interface system (windows, buttons, fields, bars, slots, tooltips, titles, scroll bars). Every shape with no background of its own is dressed with it, on every screen.
  • For one shape: Format pane, Background › Image. Dragging an image from the asset explorer onto the screen places it at its size; dropped on a shape, it becomes its background. An image from the library enters the project.
  • The stretchable frame (9-slice): the four margins, in pixels of the image, cut it into nine pieces; the cut lines show on the preview. The corners keep their size, the edges and the middle stretch or repeat. Corner size: 1, one pixel of the image for one pixel of a 1080-high screen.
  • A button's images per state: normal, hovered, pressed, disabled. A state left empty takes the normal image. Preview shows the hovered or pressed button in the editor.
  • Gauges as images: a background image and a fill image, cut according to the value without being stretched, in the chosen direction (Fills).
  • An icon in a sheet: Pick from the sheet… shows the whole image; draw the rectangle you want on it, or give the size of a cell and click the cell.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: When a system is updated
items.text: When a new version of WorldMint updates a system, its screens you have not modified are replaced by the new version. Those you have modified are kept as they are, and the log says so. Removing a system removes its unmodified screens; its modified screens stay in My game. Everything can be undone.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: The screens delivered by the systems
items.text:
Activate a system in the Systems panel: its screens arrive in the list, in its group. Screen names are the same in every language (scripts use them), so they are written here as the editor shows them.

System Its screens Menu Écran titre (title screen), Pause, Options, Rejoindre (join), Personnage (character). The layout setting of the title screen and the pause (centered, left, bottom) replaces the screen by the chosen template, as long as you have not modified it. Round Lancer la partie, Attente des joueurs, Compte à rebours, Départ, Bandeau de la partie, Annonces, Tableau entre deux manches, Classement final. Shop, Dialogue Boutique; Dialogue. Inventory Inventaire, Barre rapide (quick bar). Crafting Fabrication, Fabrication détaillée, Fabrication en cours. Quest log Journal de quêtes, Suivi des quêtes, Annonces des quêtes. Equipment Équipement, Atelier de l'équipement, Message de l'équipement. Progression Barre d'expérience, Gain d'expérience, Passage de niveau, Messages de la progression, Fiche du personnage. Map Grande carte, Lieux découverts, Mini-carte ronde, Mini-carte carrée, Boussole, Boussole en bas. Building Catalogue de construction, Mode construction. Knowledge Savoir, Annonce du savoir. Health bar, Stamina Barre de vie; Barre d'endurance. Needs Besoins, Message des besoins. Status effects Effets en cours, Infobulle d'effet. Gathering, Interaction Invite de la collecte, Message de la collecte; Invite d'interaction. Ranged weapons Arme et munitions. Day and night Horloge (clock). Passage Attente du groupe.

A few windows are still drawn by their system's code (for example the menu of an inventory slot and an item's description): they stay listed under The game screen, where you can move and resize them, but not format them like a screen.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Ready-made windows: Menu, Dialogue, Inventory, Shop, Quest log, Map
items.text: Six systems give the game its most common windows, without a script. They are activated in the Systems panel (Developer mode), and their screens are formatted in the screen editor. While they are open, the world can stop: the player, enemies, rolling objects and game time wait, and only clicks on the window count. All of them also work with a gamepad and a keyboard (see Gamepad and keyboard), and a saved game keeps them as they were (see What a saved game keeps).
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Menu: the title screen and the pause
items.text:
• The title screen: at start, the game's title and the Play, Options and Quit buttons, over the stopped, darkened game. The title is the one from the game settings (Window section), or the one written in the Title shown setting.
  • The pause: Escape (or Start on a gamepad) stops the game and opens Resume, Options and Quit. Escape closes it.
  • The options, arranged in sections, one per tab: Sound (the master volume and each group of the sound mixer, in steps of 10%), Display (the language of a translated game, the graphics) and Controls (the key of each control: click it, then press the new one; Escape cancels). A section too long for the screen (many sound groups, many controls) scrolls with the mouse wheel or the gamepad: the window never overflows.
  • The menu's texts are in French or English, after the player's language.

Its five screens (Écran titre, Pause, Options, Rejoindre, Personnage) are formatted in the screen editor. Its settings and events are in the Menu system reference.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Dialogue: a character who talks
items.text:
Place the Dialogue system on a character: they talk when the player uses them (E). Their lines show one by one in a window at the bottom of the screen, under their name, with the player's answers as buttons.

A dialogue reads like a flowchart. It is a list of rows, in order, of four kinds:

  • The character says: a line. Without answers, it has a Next button (or End when nothing follows).
  • The player answers: an answer, placed under the line it answers. There can be as many as needed. An answer can be offered only under a condition: if the player carries an item (10 "Gold" to pay a toll), if a mark is set, if they already talked to the character.
  • Test: a question the dialogue asks the game, to choose what comes next. Either yes or no: does the player carry a Key?, is the mark "met_the_king" set?, with a next step for yes and one for no. Or by a number: how many talks already finished?, how much Gold do they carry?.
  • Test exit: under a "by a number" test, where to go from a given number on. 0, 1, 2, 3, then 4: the last one counts for "4 and more".

The dialogue starts at the first row. Each row says where to go next: another row's label (a word naming it, such as friend), fin, or nothing for the next row. A row that has a label starts another branch: the talk stops before it instead of going into it.

A row can also set a mark, a word the whole game remembers (the king blesses, the guard recognises it later), and send an event such as door.open. A Trigger rule "When the event door.open" on the door then makes it disappear, without writing code.

A guard who loses patience at every visit, then lets in who has the key:

Row Kind Content Then 1 Test Do they carry a Key? yes: in; no: the next row 2 Test By the talks already finished its exits 3 to 7 Test exits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and more key, again, nothing, enough, dungeon 8 The character says key: "You need a key." 9 The character says again: "You again?" … 12 The character says dungeon: "To the dungeon!" (sends dungeon) 13 The character says in: "Ah, you have the key. Come in."

The Show the map button, in the character's properties, shows it as a flowchart, from top to bottom: Start, one box per line, one diamond per test, a named arrow for each answer or exit ("Yes", "No", "4 and more"), and an End at the end of each branch. Branches spread side by side; drag to move the map, and zoom with Ctrl + wheel. Show all fits it whole in the window, Actual size puts it back to its size.

The dialogue can also be changed in the map, and Ctrl+Z undoes it:

  • drag the circle at the start of an arrow onto a box to make it lead there (or to an End); dropped in the void, it offers to create the step it will lead to;
  • right-click the background: add a line, a yes or no test, or a test by a number;
  • right-click a box: add an answer (or an exit), or delete the step;
  • right-click an arrow's name: make it lead to the end, or delete the answer or exit.

The texts themselves are changed in the properties: a click on a box brings you there. In the map, a label that leads nowhere shows in red. In the properties list, rows are ordered with the Move up and Move down arrows.

Its settings are in the Dialogue system reference.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Inventory: the window
items.text: The Inventory system now has its window: the I key (or Back on a gamepad) opens and closes it. It shows one slot per kind of item carried, with its quantity, in a grid; beyond four rows, it scrolls with the mouse wheel. A click on a slot tells the game (inventaire.choisi): eating an apple or equipping a sword is something to ask the agent. See the Inventory system reference.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Shop: a merchant who sells
items.text:
Place the Shop system on a merchant: when the player uses them (E), a window opens with their items, their prices, the player's money, and a Buy button per item. The world stops while shopping (setting Stop the game while shopping).

The money is a kind of inventory item, such as "Gold" or "Coin": the player picks it up, receives it as a quest reward, like any item. The Money setting says which one this merchant accepts.

What they sell is a list, in the merchant's properties, one item per row:

Setting of an item What it says Item The kind of item sold, as the inventory stores it, such as "Sword". They sell it Unticked, the merchant only buys it back: no Buy button. How many per purchase 10 for a quiver of 10 arrows. Price What one purchase costs, in the merchant's money. Stock at the start How many purchases before they run out: 1 for a unique sword, 0 for no limit. Buy-back What the merchant pays if the player sells them one: a Sell button appears. 0: they buy none.

Buying takes the price from the inventory, then gives the item; selling does the reverse, one item at a time. The window says it clearly when money is missing ("You need 5 more Gold."), when the inventory has no room left (the player then keeps their money), or when an item is sold out.

Each purchase and each sale tells the game (boutique.achat, boutique.vente): a sound, a quest step ("Buy a sword"), a Trigger rule.

A merchant who also has a Dialogue talks first. The player uses them: the conversation opens, alone. On its last line, next to End, a Show me your goods button closes the conversation and opens the shop. Nothing to untick, nothing to write. To put the way into the shop elsewhere in the conversation (an answer "Show me your weapons" in the middle), give that answer the event boutique.ouvrir with the next step fin: the Dialogue then does not add its own button. Unticking Opens when the player uses it also removes that button: the shop then only opens through boutique.ouvrir.

Its settings are in the Shop system reference.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Quest log: quests that move on by themselves
items.text:
The Quest log system is for the whole game. Its quests are written in its setting The quests and their steps, on the system's card in the Systems panel: a Quest row, then its Step rows, in order.

A quest has a title, a description, and a start:

  • when the game starts;
  • when an event happens: a Dialogue answer ("I accept" sends wolves.accepted), a Trigger rule;
  • when a mark is set by a Dialogue;
  • when another quest ends: a chain of quests.

A step says what to do ("Defeat 3 wolves") and what ends it:

  • an event, as many times as needed, and only for the object named if one is given: sante.mort for "Wolf", 3 times, counts three wolves defeated (and not the bear); dialogue.fin for "Miller", a talk with him finished; zone.entree for a zone, a place reached;
  • a mark set by a Dialogue;
  • items carried: 3 "Wolf pelt" in the inventory;
  • items handed over: on an event (dialogue.fin for "Miller"), if the player carries 3 "Wolf pelt", the inventory takes them back and the step is done. Otherwise, an announcement says how many are missing ("Not enough: Wolf pelt 2/3").

Steps are done one after the other (the log does not reveal what comes next), or all at the same time if Steps one after the other is unticked. When all are done, the quest ends and gives its reward (items, such as 50 "Gold"). A finished quest or step can also set a mark (the miller thanks the player, his Dialogue sees it) and send an event (a Trigger rule makes the bridge appear).

A quest can also fail (setting Fails): when an event happens (sante.mort for "Merchant": the merchant to escort is dead), when a mark is set, or when time runs out (Time to finish it, in seconds of play: the tracker and the log show what is left). The player can abandon it from the log (Abandon button, a second press confirms), unless The player can abandon it is unticked. A failed or abandoned quest gives no reward; it can set its own mark and send its own event (the miller complains), and, if Can be taken up again is ticked, what gives it gives it again from the start.

What the player sees:

  • an announcement at the top of the screen for each new quest, each step done and each quest finished (with its reward), failed or abandoned;
  • the current step, on the right of the screen, with the progress ("Defeat 3 wolves (2/3)");
  • the log, with the J key (or → on a gamepad): the quests in progress with their steps, then the finished ones, then the failed or abandoned ones. It scrolls with the mouse wheel, and the same key closes it.

A miller who asks to hunt the wolves:

Row Kind Content Starts or ends 1 Quest "The mill's wolves", reward 50 Gold when the event wolves.accepted happens (the miller's "I accept" answer) 2 Step "Defeat 3 wolves", sets the mark wolves_hunted the event sante.mort for "Wolf", 3 times 3 Step "Go back to the miller" the event wolves.returned (the answer "Here they are", offered if the mark wolves_hunted is set)

Its settings and events are in the Quest log system reference.

No map yet

Unlike the Dialogue, quests do not have a map view yet: they are written in the settings list, and the agent can write them for you.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: What a saved game keeps
items.text:
When the game saves (a key, a checkpoint: ask the agent, which has a recipe for it), every system stores its own state in the save, and takes it back when loading:

System What it keeps Inventory What the player carries, kind by kind. Quest log The quests started, finished, failed or abandoned, the steps done, what is already counted ("2 wolves out of 3"), the time left to a timed quest. Shop What each merchant has left of the items with a limited stock. Dialogue The marks set, and the conversations already had with each one.

The player therefore goes on where they were: in the middle of a quest, after a purchase. Items given back when loading do not make the pickup sound.

The game also keeps the world: what the game changed in every scene visited (an object hidden, moved, destroyed or copied, a light, a door opened, the camera...) comes back as it was when loading. Nothing to do for it: see Saved games.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Map: the minimap, the big map and its markers
items.text:
The Map system is for the whole game, and is also placed on the objects to mark. Once activated:

  • the minimap, in a corner of the screen (bottom right by default), shows the world around the player, seen from above. The player is the white arrow in the middle; a small N marks north. It can be round or square, bigger or smaller, show nearer or farther, and turn with the player instead of keeping north at the top;
  • the big map opens with the M key (or ↓ on a gamepad) and closes the same way: the whole scene, with the player and the markers, their name written under them. The wheel zooms around the mouse, holding the mouse drags the map, and so do the gamepad's left stick and the walking keys. On a gamepad, the right trigger (RT) zooms in and the left trigger (LT) zooms out while held; on a keyboard, Page Up and Page Down. They are two controls of the game, Zoom the big map in and Zoom the big map out, whose keys can be changed in the Game tab. The world stops meanwhile (setting Stop the game while the big map is open).

The picture of the map is taken by the game itself: when the game starts, it photographs the scene from above (the terrain, its waters, its plants, the buildings), without the player or the characters, who move. It can be replaced by a drawn map (setting Drawn map): by default, it covers the same square of the world as the game's picture; otherwise, you give its west edge, its north edge and its side, in meters.

A marker, without code: place the Map system on an object (a town, a cave, a chest). In its properties:

Setting What it says Name on the map Written under the marker on the big map. Empty: the object's name, without number. Shape of the marker Circle, diamond, triangle, square, star, or an image (a sword icon for the forge). Color of the marker, Size of the marker Its color (it tints an image), and its size: 2 for a town. When it shows on the map Always; once discovered up close, when the player comes within the discovery distance (a message announces it; a saved game keeps the places discovered); or hidden, except as a quest objective. Objective of the quest The title of a quest: while it is in progress (or only during the step given), this marker is its objective.

Placed on a folder, the system gives a single marker for everything it holds, in place of the folder.

What marks itself: merchants (Shop system, a golden diamond) and characters who talk (Dialogue system, a light blue circle), named after their shop or their character. Placing Map on one of them chooses its look.

Quest objectives: during a step of the Quest log (above) that aims at named objects ("Defeat 3 wolves", for Wolf), their markers are ringed with the color of the objectives, even when usually hidden; on the minimap, a far objective stays at its edge, in its direction. The Quest log is not changed: the map only listens to what it announces.

The game can react when the big map opens or closes (carte.ouverte) and when a marker is discovered (carte.decouvert); a Trigger rule or a Dialogue answer can reveal a place (carte.reveler), like a villager who points to the cave. Its settings and events are in the Map system reference.

No fog of war yet

The parts of the world where the player has not been yet are not hidden in black yet: only markers wait to be discovered.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: The Interface system: the look of everything shown
items.text:
The Interface system gives its style to the whole game interface, from one place. It applies to the whole game and is not placed on objects.

  1. Systems panel, Systems section: Activate under Interface (see The game's systems and settings).
  2. Open its card: its settings apply at once to everything the game shows. A color is chosen by clicking its swatch, which opens a color picker.
Setting What it changes Panel background color Menus, windows, lists. Button and field background color Buttons and text fields. Accent color: hovered button, selected field, scroll bar What is under the mouse or chosen. Text color All texts. Text size (share of the screen height) The text keeps the same relative size whatever the window. Corner rounding (share of the screen height, 0: square corners) The shape of panels, buttons and fields. Background opacity (0: transparent, 1: solid) Lets the game show through the backgrounds, or not. Alert color A refusal flagged for a moment: the slot of an item too heavy to pick up. Image theme: the interface pack One image per kind of element (windows, buttons, fields, bars, slots, tooltips, titles, scroll bars), and variants per role (the health bar, the inventory slot). A kind without an image keeps the color drawing.

The exact values and their limits are in the Interface system reference.

These settings are the game's theme: every shape with no background of its own takes them. A background, a color or a style chosen for a shape in the screen editor wins over the theme (see The theme, and the background you choose). Apply the game theme, in Manage styles, brings the theme's styles among the game's styles, to set them one by one.

A script can also give an element its own color or size: it wins over the theme. To keep control of the style from one place, ask the agent to use the theme and the styles rather than colors written in the scripts. Without the Interface system, the interface keeps its original look.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Asking the agent
items.text:
A few requests:

  • "Add a title screen and a pause." The agent then activates the Menu system.
  • "The blacksmith offers to repair the sword; if the player accepts, the workshop door opens." The agent places a Dialogue on the blacksmith and a Trigger rule on the door.
  • "The blacksmith sells a sword for 30 gold coins and potions, and buys back wolf pelts." The agent places a Shop on the blacksmith.
  • "The miller asks to hunt three wolves, for 50 gold coins." The agent writes the quest in the Quest log, and the answer that gives it in the miller's Dialogue.
  • "At the start of the game, ask the player for their name, then show "Welcome, [name]!"."
  • "A chat window at the bottom left, with a scrolling history."
  • "Give the interface a dark and gold style." The agent then changes the settings of the Interface system, not every script.
  • "Add a score at the top right and a timer at the top center." The agent draws a screen in My game: you then adjust it with the mouse.
  • "On the title screen, make the buttons golden pills and remove the Options button." The agent changes the screen delivered by the Menu, as you would in the editor.

What the agent does: it draws your screens (with their shapes, styles and buttons), changes the look of the screens delivered by the systems, sets the theme of the Interface system, and writes the scripts that fill your screens (game.screen_set, game.screen_list, game.on_screen_action). It never changes a system's code: it goes through its screens, its settings and its events. Each of its changes can be undone with Ctrl+Z, and a delivered screen it changed keeps Back to the system's version.

To check a menu, the agent runs the game without a window: it sees where each element was placed, what overflows a list, how the texts wrap, then looks at the game's image. You can also try it yourself with Play (F5).

To go further, all the interface functions (game.hud_panel, game.hud_input...) are in the scripts reference.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Known limits
items.text:
• The preview is still small in the editor window: zoom with the Display tab, or undock the panel.
  • A style "based on" another shows its own values in the Format pane, not those it inherits.
  • A few windows are still drawn by their system's code (the menu of an inventory slot, an item's description): they move in The game screen, but are not formatted like a screen.
  • What follows the 3D world (names above heads, bubbles, markers) does not open in the editor: change a style to change its look.
path: The game interface: screens, menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Getting started
items.text: This page takes you from creating a project to a running game. Each step links to the page that details it.

items.title: 1. Create a project
items.text:
File > New project...: choose where to put it and its name ("My game" is suggested). A project is a folder that holds your whole game: its scenes, the models it uses, its settings. See Projects and scenes.

Right after, the Creation assistant offers two choices:

  • With the assistant: it asks you a few questions about your game (the story, the mood, days and nights going by, the places, the character, what one does, people to talk to, merchants, quests, a title screen...), one step at a time. Each choice tells the agent which system brings it: ticking "Buy and sell at merchants" asks it for the Shop. Next moves on, Skip skips a question, Back returns. At the end, it prepares Your request to the agent: read it, change it if you like, then Launch sends it to the agent, which first presents its plan and waits for your go-ahead before building. Save and close keeps your answers for later.
  • Start from scratch: you build yourself, or by talking directly to the agent.

The assistant reopens at any time with Game > Creation assistant...; your answers are kept in the project.

items.title: 2. The window
items.text:
• At the top: the menus (File, Edit, Select, Object, View, Game, Agent, Help), a few buttons in the middle (gizmo axes, snapping, four views, undo, redo), and on the right the Preferences (gear) and the Play button.
  • On the left: three tabs. Scene lists what is in the scene, Systems holds the game's systems and opens its controls, its interface and its settings, Scripts its scripts.
  • In the middle: the 3D view, with its tool column on the left.
  • At the bottom: the Library, your models and sounds.
  • On the right: the Properties of what is selected, and the Agent panel. Each folds with its chevron; a handle between them shares the height.
  • At the very bottom, the status bar: Library opens or closes the library, the editor's last message (a click opens the Console), and on the right the agent's state, the time of the last automatic backup, the number of selected objects and the number of objects in the scene.

Each part has its page: see The editor.

items.title: 3. Add models
items.text:
1. Add a folder of models to the library: Add a folder, then Browse or paste its path. You can also drag a folder from File Explorer onto the window.
  2. In the library, double-click a model to add it to the scene, or drag it into the 3D view, where you want it.
  3. For a simple shape: Object > Create (Cube, Sphere, Cylinder, Capsule, Plane), or right-click in the list of the Scene tab.

Double-clicked, the model arrives at the center of the view; dragged, it arrives where you drop it. The Place on ground when adding preference, on by default, then sets it on the ground. The model's file is copied into the project: your library never changes.

items.title: 4. Place objects
items.text:
• Select: click the object, in the view or in the list. Ctrl + click adds to the selection; dragging in the view draws a rectangle.
  • Move, rotate, scale: keys W, E, R, or the tool column on the left of the view, then pull the handles (the gizmo). Or type the values in the Properties, Position and size section.
  • Place on ground: End key, or the Place on ground button in the properties.
  • Look around: hold the right mouse button to orbit, the middle button to pan, the wheel to zoom, F to frame the selection.

See The 3D view.

items.title: 5. Choose the player
items.text: The game needs a character to play. Select a model (an animated character, preferably), then click Set as player in its Properties. Its properties then show its Movement, its Animations and the Player camera: see The properties.

items.title: 6. Play
items.text:
F5, or the Play button at the top right. The game opens in its own window; the editor stays open beside it. While the game runs, the player settings you change in the properties apply live. F5 or Stop closes the game.

In the game, the player moves with the game controls: by default W A S D on a QWERTY keyboard (Z Q S D on AZERTY), Left Shift to run, Space to jump, the mouse to turn the camera. Esc frees the mouse.

items.title: 7. Undo
items.text: Everything can be undone, your changes and the agent's: Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Y redoes. The same commands are in the Edit menu and as arrows in the middle of the top bar. Under each answer of the agent, Undo these changes undoes everything it did during that turn.

items.title: 8. Save
items.text: Ctrl+S saves the scene. Every 60 seconds, an automatic backup keeps a separate copy, without touching your file. If the editor closes before you saved, it offers to Recover your work on the next launch.

items.title: 9. Ask the agent
items.text: In the Agent panel, describe what you want to build and press Enter. The agent works in the scene before your eyes. See The agent.

items.title: What you need
items.text:
• Windows. WorldMint only runs on Windows for now.
  • A graphics card that supports Vulkan 1.3, with an up-to-date driver. Vulkan is what lets WorldMint draw in 3D. Recent NVIDIA, AMD and Intel graphics cards support it, as long as their driver (the card's software) is up to date. If yours is too old, WorldMint says so as soon as it opens: update the driver, from the NVIDIA, AMD or Intel website or through Windows Update, then start it again. Once the editor is open, the status bar, at the bottom of the window, shows the card in use.
  • 3D models, if you want to build with your own: .glb, .gltf, .fbx or .obj files. The editor ships none; you add their folders to the library.
  • For the agent: a Claude account (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise subscription, or usage-based billing) or a ChatGPT account for Codex. The editor installs the program that makes the link for you: see The agent.

items.title: Installing WorldMint
items.text:
WorldMint is installed with an installer, like most Windows programs. The installer will be available with the beta.

  1. Download the WorldMint installer.
  2. Run it (double-click) and follow its steps.
  3. Open WorldMint.

items.title: The first launch
items.text:
On the first launch, WorldMint creates an empty project, Mon premier jeu, in Documents\WorldMint\, and opens it. On later launches, it reopens the last scene you had open. A project is an ordinary folder, which you find in File Explorer (File > Open project folder): see Projects and scenes.

The editor uses the language of Windows, French or English. To change it: Help > Language, or the Preferences.

Then:

  1. Add your models: in the Library, at the bottom, click Add a folder, or drag a folder from File Explorer onto the editor window.
  2. Connect the agent: in the Agent panel, on the right, choose Claude or Codex, then how you want to sign in.
  3. Follow Getting started.

items.title: Where your settings are
items.text: The editor's preferences (language, theme, library folders, recent scenes) are kept in %APPDATA%\WorldMint\Editeur\preferences.json. They apply to all your projects. An API key you give the editor is kept encrypted for your Windows session.

items.title: Launch options
items.text:
For command-line users, WorldMint.exe accepts a project file (.worldmint) or scene file (.wmscene) to open, and these options:

Option Effect --project <folder or file> Opens this project, on its start scene. --scene <file> Opens this scene. --assets <folder> Adds this folder to the library for this session (the option can be repeated; your preferences keep nothing of it). --language fr or --language en Chooses the interface language. --low-power Prefers the most power-saving graphics card (a laptop with two cards). --no-preferences Starts with default preferences, without reading or writing yours.

items.title: Light and shadows
items.text: A scene's light comes from the sun, the sky and the ground, and from the lights you place. It is set in the game settings: deselect everything (or click the game's line, at the very top of the Scene tab), Sky and light section.

items.title: The sun, the sky and the ground
items.text:
Setting Effect Sun color, Sun intensity The color and strength of its light. A white surface facing the sun takes exactly its color. Sun direction Where it shines from (X, Y, Z): positive Y, it is up. Shadows go the opposite way. Sky The color of the sky's light: it lights everything, even in the shade, and is reflected by what is smooth or metal. Light from the ground The light bounced by the ground, which lights the underside of objects. Exposure How much light reaches the image, as on a camera. With automatic exposure, it adds to what the eye chose. Automatic exposure Like an eye getting used to it: when you walk into a dark place (a house lit by a small window, a cave), the image brightens over a second or two, and comes back when you walk out, without dazzling. In sunlight, the image does not change. On by default, also for scenes made before it. Brighten up to How many times brighter the image can get in the dark: 1 never, 4 by default (a dark room becomes readable without turning into daylight). Darken up to How many times darker it can get under a very strong light: 1 never (default: a sunny scene stays as you set it), 2 to 4 for a glare when walking out of a cave. Adaptation time The time the eye takes to get used to the dark: 1.5 s by default; it gets used to light three times faster. 0: at once.

In the editor, the views show the image once the eye is used to it; you see it brighten little by little in the game. A passage to another scene or a teleport arrives already used to it, without a flash. Night stays night: with the day and night cycle (or a script that lowers the sun), the eye only brightens what is darker than the current daylight; a dark house at noon is brightened, nightfall is not. Scripts set it with game.set_environment (auto_exposure, auto_exposure_brighten, auto_exposure_darken, auto_exposure_seconds).

items.title: Sun shadows
items.text:
Objects, characters, terrain and plants cast their shadow in the sun: on the ground, on the water and on each other, and also on the smoke, dust, rain or snow passing below them, and on decals. So does the object a character holds. Shadows are soft at their edges and don't flicker when the camera moves.

Setting Effect Sun shadows Unticked: no sun shadows, lighter rendering. Shadow quality For the sun and the lights (fires included). Depends on the computer: low on an integrated graphics chip (most laptops), high on a graphics card. High: sharp all the way. Medium: one shadow slice less in the distance, fewer lights with shadows. Low: blurrier up close, lighter to draw. Off: no shadows at all, from the sun or the lights, the lightest. In the editor, it never goes above the View quality (Preferences); the game follows it. The player can also choose their own in the game menu (Shadows row). Shadow distance How far around the camera they are drawn (150 m by default). Beyond that, they fade out gently. The further it is, the less sharp they are up close: for a game seen up close (a dungeon), 50 to 100 m is enough. Shadow softness Softens their edge as under a real sun: the shadow stays sharp at the foot of an object and gets softer further from it (a pole's shadow, sharp at its base, blurred at its end). It is the size of the sun in the sky, in degrees: 0 sharp (default), 0.5 the real sun, 2 to 4 a hazy sky, up to 10 very soft. Wind strength The wind in the plants sown by the terrain, from 0 (dead calm) to 1 (strong wind); 0.3 by default, a breeze. The base of the plants stays fixed, the top bends, and gusts sweep across the field in the wind's direction; each plant kind follows it by its Sway in the wind (grass a lot, a tree a little). Their shadows and far versions move with them. Off in Low quality. Wind direction Where it blows to, in degrees: 0 towards +x, 90 towards +z, like the direction of the waves.

Shadows also show in the editor's view, except in wireframe only.

If the game is slow on a laptop

Lower the Shadow distance, or set Shadow quality to Low, or Off as a last resort. On an integrated chip, Depends on the computer already picks Low. Shadow softness costs a little more in High and Medium (the penumbra is searched at each point); in Low, it is only a fixed blur, almost free.

items.title: Fog and glow
items.text:
In the distance, the scene always fades gently into the Background color instead of being cut off: that is the horizon fog, with no setting. For more, in Sky and light:

Setting Effect Fog distance A fog over the whole scene: at this distance, it hides almost everything in its color. 0: none. A light mist: 300 to 800 m; a thick fog: 40 to 100 m. It also hides what is too far to be drawn. Fog color The color of what is in the fog, and of the sky behind it. Fog altitude, Thins out with height A fog that stays low (a valley, a swamp, the mist over the sea): at its altitude it has the set thickness, below it gets thicker, above it halves every so many meters (5 to 30). 0: the same everywhere. Glow of bright lights A soft glow around what shines very brightly: a material giving off light, the sun shining on water or metal, a lamp close by. 1 by default, discreet; 0: none. Sand or snow in full sun don't get it. Color grading The tint of the whole image, like grading a film, through a color table for each look: Soft realistic (the one of a new project: a filmic curve for depth, dense but open blacks, noticeable darkened corners and sharpening, a fine grain, no tint), Neutral (changes nothing; a project made before the looks keeps it, its image does not change), Cinema (marked: a strong filmic curve, teal shadows, warm highlights, dark corners, a visible grain), Realistic (a light film contrast), Stylized (bold colors), European city (soft, slightly cool), American city (warm, golden), Seaside (bright, turquoise shadows). Grading strength sets how much, from 0 to 1. Almost free, at every quality. The agent sets it with world_set (colorGrade, colorGradeStrength). Corner shading (ambient occlusion) Darkens corners, the foot of walls, the underside of balconies and the inside of windows, where less sky reaches: 0 none, 1 (default) the quality's own, 2 twice as strong. Only the sky's light darkens, never the sun or the lamps. It is worked out from what is seen on screen: at half the image size on Medium quality, full size on High and Ultra, off on Low. With ray tracing, its rays darken the corners instead (they also see what is off screen): two rays per point on Medium and High, looking for an obstacle within 3 m. The setting acts in both cases: with rays, it scales their reach and the strength; 0 turns both off. The agent sets it with world_set (ambientOcclusion), a script with game.set_environment (ambient_occlusion). Film grain A light film grain that moves all the time, mostly in the midtones: 0 (default) none, 0.2 to 0.4 subtle, 1 strong. Off on Low quality. The agent sets it with world_set (filmGrain). Motion blur What moves fast in front of the camera blurs along its motion: 0 (default) none, 0.5 a cinema camera's shutter (good for a driving game: strong at high speed, nothing on the car the camera follows), 1 very strong. Off on Low quality. The agent sets it with world_set (motionBlur). Depth of field, Focus distance, Out-of-focus blur Like a camera lens: sharp at the set distance (10 m by default), blurrier and blurrier in front and behind, up to the set blur (0 to 1). For a cutscene or a close-up view. Off on Low quality, off by default. The agent sets it with world_set (depthOfField, focusDistance, focusBlur).

Adding a color look. The shipped looks are in config/couleurs.json, next to WorldMint. For your game, add your own in the scene (ask the agent, or in the scene file, environment.colorGradeLooks), in the same format: {"id": "dusk", "name": {"fr": "Crépuscule", "en": "Dusk"}, "temperature": 0.4, "tint": 0, "saturation": 1.1, "contrast": 1.05, "shadows": [0.02, 0, 0.03], "highlights": [1.1, 0.95, 0.85]}. Temperature and tint from -1 to 1, saturation from 0 to 2, contrast from 0.5 to 2, shadows from -0.2 to 0.2 (a color added), highlights from 0.5 to 1.5 (a color multiplied). It then shows in the Color grading list; a look with the same id as a shipped one replaces it for this game. A look also keeps the camera look's settings, all without effect by default: curve (the filmic curve, 0 to 1: depth in the midtones, dense but open blacks, no tint), exposureEv (the compensation, -3 to 3 stops), bloom (the glow multiplied, 0 to 4), sharpen (sharpness, 0 to 1), vignette, vignetteRadius and vignetteSoftness (darkened corners), grain and grainSize (the grain multiplied, and its size), lut and lutStrength (a project .cube table, and its strength). Sharpness, darkened corners, glow and grain show in the image, scaled by the look's strength; sharpness is off on Low quality, and with FSR it sets FSR's own sharpness (the larger of the two) rather than adding a second one. Keep sharpness at 0.25 or less with foliage or wires: higher makes them shimmer. The compensation (exposureEv) is added to the scene's exposure: water, fog, FSR and auto exposure all see it. The .cube table (lut, a path relative to the project, "looks/night.cube") applies after the rest of the look, on the screen color (sRGB), blended by lutStrength, then by the look's strength; it is baked into the same 32³ table as the other settings, at no extra cost for the graphics card. WorldMint reads 3D tables in the Adobe and Resolve format (LUT_3D_SIZE from 2 to 65, including 17, 32, 33 and 64; DOMAIN_MIN, DOMAIN_MAX, TITLE, comments) and resamples them. A 1D table, or a file that is malformed, missing or over 16 MB, is refused with a message in French and English (in the log); the look then renders without the table. A changed file is read again on its own. No shipped look changes the color of lights: windows stay white or yellow according to their temperature.

The look cycle (by the hour). The image's look can follow the sky's hour, like GTA's timecycle, without touching the light: a timeline of keys {hour, look, hold, fade}, in the scene (environment.lookCycle; the agent sets it with world_set). A key keeps its look for its hold (in hours) after its hour; the next key's look comes in through a fade (in hours) that ends exactly at that key's hour. Without a fade of its own, the cycle's fade; without a cycle fade, all the time left after the hold; a fade of 0 switches at once. The last key joins the first over midnight. Two looks mix setting by setting (curve, contrast, colors, darkened corners, sharpening, grain, exposure compensation), and the color table is only recomputed when the mix has moved enough to be seen: a sped-up day shows no jump. For example, Soft realistic by day and Cinema at dusk: {"keys": [{"hour": 7, "look": "realiste_doux", "hold": 10}, {"hour": 19.5, "look": "cinema", "hold": 2, "fade": 1.5}]}. Without keys nothing changes: the look chosen in Color grading stays fixed. With keys the cycle replaces it (the strength still applies). Looks per weather (weather: {"weather": "rain", "look": "neutre", "amount": 0.5}, mixed by the weather's intensity) are stored and checked; they will apply once the scene has a live weather. Districts, interiors and tunnels come later, as does the timeline in the editor.

From a script, game.set_environment also changes the camera look during play: game.set_environment({motion_blur = 0.6}) when getting into a car, {motion_blur = 0} when getting out; color_grade, color_grade_strength, film_grain, depth_of_field, focus_distance, focus_blur the same way.

items.title: Volumetric fog: rays of light
items.text:
Turn on Volumetric fog (in Sky and light) so that sunlight shows in the air, with the shadow of whatever hides it: rays between trees and through windows, a darker mist under the leaves, a brighter one when looking toward the sun. The fog keeps its Distance and Color (it hides as much as before); it also works without fog, thanks to the air.

Setting Effect Rays in the air A slightly hazy air that shows the rays even without fog. 0: none; 0.2 by default, mostly when looking toward the sun; 1: very strong, from the side too. In a room, a little fog (dust) shows the rays from the windows. Scattering toward the sun How much brighter the mist shines when looking toward the sun. 0: the same everywhere; 0.3 by default; 0.6 to 0.9: a strong glow around the sun, bright rays against the light.

Rays need a sun low enough to pass between things (a Sun direction whose height, the second value, is small), and something that casts shadows: trees, walls. With ray tracing, the shadow in the mist comes from rays, through the gaps in the leaves; without it, from shadow maps: the same look.

Depending on the computer

In Low quality (an integrated chip), the fog stays the usual one, without its rays. In Medium (the editor's views) and High, it is light: a few hundredths of a millisecond per frame on a recent graphics card, the same whatever the image size.

items.title: Fog in one area only: the fog volume
items.text:
The fog of Sky and light covers the whole map. For a mist that stays in its place (a valley floor, an undergrowth, a marsh, the smoke of a cave), choose Create > Fog volume: an invisible box that the fog fills, and that fades out towards its edges. Move it and scale it like an object; several volumes can overlap. Its settings are those of the Fog volume system: its Visibility (at this distance you can hardly see anything), its Color, its Soft edges, and Thicker at the bottom for a mist that stays on the ground.

With volumetric fog on, the volume catches the sun's rays and shadows: a volume in a forest, with no fog in Sky and light (Distance at 0), shows rays there only. In Low quality, and far from the camera (beyond the shadow distance), it is drawn without its shadows, but always in its place.

items.title: Sun rays without mist: the glowing air
items.text:
For sun rays in a forest or a room, like dust lit by the sun, without a veil over the rest, choose Create > Glowing air (or, in a fog volume's properties, Kind: Glowing air (rays only)). It is an almost invisible air: it only shows where the sun crosses it, mostly when looking toward the sun, and the air in the shade stays clear. Its Air visibility sets how strong the rays are (200 m by default; 100 m for strong rays, 400 m for a light trace); it has no colour (it takes the sun's). It needs volumetric fog on, in High or Medium quality, and a sun low enough to pass between foliage or walls; in Low quality it does not show.

You want Choose Sun rays in the forest, through a window Glowing air The mist of a valley, a marsh, smoke Fog volume

items.title: Placed lights
items.text:
A lamp, a torch, a street lamp, a lit window, a spotlight on a stage: Create > Light (in the scene list). It appears a little above where you look; move it like an object.

  • A Bulb lights all around it; a Spotlight lights in a cone, toward the bottom of the object: turn it to aim.
  • Its Color is the object's. Its Intensity is its strength at 1 m: it falls off with distance, and fades out gently at its Range.
  • Light temperature: a ready-made tint, that of a real lamp. Sodium (2,000 K), the orange of street lamps; Warm white (3,000 K), a bulb; Neutral (4,000 K); Cold (5,500 K), bluish. It changes the object's Color, which you can still set by hand.
  • Switches on at night: the light follows the sun. Off during the day, it fades in when the sun goes below the horizon (it starts when the sun is 2° above it and is full 6° below, the end of dusk) and goes out in the morning. For a town's street lamps, shop windows and windows. It follows the sun's direction as it is (World, Environment): with a high sun, it stays off. Both heights are set in the environment: Lights on: sun height and Full light: sun height. With the Day and night system, it also follows the fading daylight: it switches on at nightfall, even while the moon stays above the horizon. With the realistic sky, it follows the real sun at the hour of the sky (not the moon, nor the sun set in the environment): on at dusk, off at dawn, at the same two heights.
  • Opening hours of the light: the light is on only between its Light on at and Light off at hours (to the quarter hour), at the hour of the realistic sky (World, Sky), which moves on during the game: the ceiling lights of a shop, the sign of a bar. A range can go past midnight (10 pm to 6 am). With Switches on at night, it is on at night and within the range. Without the realistic sky, the hour is unknown: it stays on. The hour is read again every frame, nothing is rebuilt. A glowing material has the same settings: Glow at night and Opening hours of the glow.
  • There can be many: each point of the image only computes the lights that reach it. Keep ranges short (a room: 5 to 10 m), that is what costs.
  • Light's shadows: what it lights casts its shadow. Only a few lights at a time get them, the closest to the camera (six spotlights, or one bulb, in low quality; twice as many in high). Keep them for the ones that matter.
  • Shadow softness (with its shadows): the size of what gives the light, in meters. 0 sharp, 0.05 a bare bulb, 0.3 a lantern or a globe. As in the sun, the shadow stays sharp at the foot of an object and gets softer further from it.
  • For them to show, it takes a bit of night: lower the Sun intensity and darken the Sky and the Light from the ground.
  • They light everything around them: objects and terrain, but also water (a lamp at the edge of a lake is reflected in it), smoke, dust, rain and snow passing near them, and decals. Fire, sparks and magic make their own light: lights don't change them.

items.title: The light of fires and effects
items.text:
A fire, an explosion, magic, sparks or the flash of a hit light up what is around them: each carries its own light, with nothing to place next to it. It follows the effect, takes its colour (a blue fire lights in blue), grows with its Size, comes on with it and goes out after its last flames. A fire's light flickers and moves a little with the flames; an explosion's is a flash that dies out in less than a second; magic's sways slowly.

Fire, explosions and magic cast shadows: a cube next to a campfire casts its shadow on the ground and on the wall behind it, as soft as the width of the flames. Sparks and hits, too brief, have none. The object carrying the effect (the logs of a campfire, the head of a torch) casts no shadow from its own light.

In the effect's properties (Particle effect system):

  • Effect light: With its shadows (default), Without shadows (the light alone, lighter), or None (the effect is only drawn).
  • Light strength: multiplied; 0.5 for a discreet glow, 2 for a blaze that lights the whole camp.

These lights count with the placed lights: the closest to the camera first, within the same limit (and the same shadow limit). They follow the Shadow quality, show in the editor's view while you set the effect, and change nothing in the game: only the image.

In the game, the Trigger switches them on, off (Switch a light on, Switch a light off, in turn) or changes their color: a lever lighting a lamp, an alarm turning red. Scripts do it with game.light and game.set_light (see the scripts reference). Hiding a light switches it off too.

When the game saves, the lights go into the save: a lamp switched on or off, recoloured or made brighter or dimmer during the game comes back as it was when loading, with nothing to write (see Saved games).

items.title: Rendering quality
items.text:
At startup, WorldMint picks a rendering quality for the computer: Low on an integrated graphics chip, High on a graphics card. Settings set to Depends on the computer follow it. To try the other one, start the game with --qualite basse or --qualite haute.

It also sets the terrain: in Low, the relief is simplified a little sooner in the distance, a large map's detail loads up to 500 m instead of 1 km, and plants stop at 60 % of their distance (see The terrain).

items.title: Hosting your own lobby
items.text: The lobby is the small service that helps a game's players find each other. By default, every game made with WorldMint uses WorldMint's, shared by every game. This page explains when to host your own, and how.

items.title: Do you need it?
items.text:
Most of the time, no. WorldMint's lobby is enough for most games: each game has its own identifier, and its players only see its servers. There is nothing to install or pay for.

Hosting your own lobby makes sense if you want:

  • independence: your game no longer depends on a service you do not run;
  • a region close to your players: a server in America or Asia for an audience there (the relay benefits most);
  • your own relay: the bandwidth of relayed games is yours, you watch it and grow it as you like.

items.title: What the lobby does
items.text:
• The public server list of your game (the List tab of the "Join a game" screen).
  • Short codes, like K7P-2QMX (the Code tab): easy to read out to a friend.
  • Getting through home routers (NAT traversal): it carries the messages while two games connect to each other, without opening a port.
  • The relay (TURN): when no router lets the connection through, the game goes through it. It stays encrypted end to end: the relay cannot read it.

The game itself never goes through the lobby, except through the relay. The lobby asks for no account; it sees the IP address of whoever talks to it and forgets it quickly (see CONFIDENTIALITE.md in the kit).

items.title: What it costs
items.text: A small rented Linux server (a "VPS"): about €5 a month from a host such as OVHcloud, Scaleway, Netcup or Hetzner; the smallest plan is enough. You also need a domain name (about €10 a year), or a free name from duckdns.org to try it out. Allow one hour the first time.

items.title: The steps
items.text:
The kit ships with the editor: in WorldMint's folder, outils\salon (by default %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\WorldMint\outils\salon). It holds the lobby program, its install script and its guide, LISEZMOI.md (in French), which details each step:

  1. rent the server (Ubuntu 24.04 or Debian 12);
  2. choose a name for the lobby, for example lobby.my-game.com;
  3. point that name to the server's address;
  4. copy the folder to the server and run the script: it installs everything (the lobby, HTTPS and its free certificate, the relay, the firewall) and ends with "Le service répond" (the service answers).

items.title: The field to fill in the editor
items.text:
Select nothing: the Properties show the game settings (so does the Game settings panel). In the Multiplayer section ("Several players" on):

  1. type your lobby's address in Lobby service, for example https://lobby.my-game.com;
  2. click Test the lobby: the editor asks the lobby whether it answers, without freezing. It says "The lobby answers (2 servers online)", "No answer: check the address" or "This is not a WorldMint lobby";
  3. export the game (and its dedicated server): they will use your lobby.

Empty field: WorldMint's lobby (the grey hint says "WorldMint's own"). The address must start with https://. For a test on your PC only, run python salon.py --ecoute 127.0.0.1 --port 8470 in the kit's folder, then put http://127.0.0.1:8470 in the field (http is only accepted towards this PC). Each change is undone with Ctrl+Z, and the agent can set it too if you give it the address.

items.title: What if it goes down?
items.text: If your lobby stops answering, the List and Code tabs say so, and getting through home routers no longer happens. Joining a game by its address always works: the game does not go through the lobby. Run the install script again on the server; it can be run as many times as needed, safely.

items.title: Materials
items.text:
A material says what a surface is made of: stone, wood, metal, grass, sand, snow... Its color, whether it is smooth or matte, whether it is metal, its relief and the light it gives off. It is a file of the project, kept in the materials/ folder: you create it once, put it on as many objects as you like, and changing it changes them all.

WorldMint ships a small starter library made of real royalty-free textures (ambientCG, CC0): Snow, Rock, Grass, Forest floor, Sand, Mud, Dirt, Cobblestones, Wooden planks, Brushed metal. Choosing one copies it into your project, with its images.

A material copied by hand

A .wmmat file copied into the project's materials/ folder while the editor is open (with its images) is read as soon as it is asked for: when the materials list opens, or when the agent names it. No need to reopen the project.

items.title: The material of an object
items.text:
Select an object (a model or a base shape): its properties have a Material section.

Setting Effect Material The model's own keeps its own colors. Otherwise, a material of the project, or one from the Library (copied into the project). New material Creates a material, with your name, put on the selected objects.

A material shows a preview on a sphere, under the light of the scene, and its settings:

Setting Effect Name The name you see in the lists. Color Tints the color image (white: as is). Roughness 0: smooth and shiny, like a mirror. 1: matte, like stone. Metal 0: stone, wood, plastic. 1: metal, which reflects its color. Pattern size The size of one repeat of the image, in meters. Placement On the model: the image follows the model's texture coordinates. Without stretching: it is laid by the world, at the same size on every face, even on an enlarged shape. The right choice for walls, floors and rocks. Image relief The strength of the relief map: 0 removes it, 2 doubles it. DirectX normal (Y flipped) The relief map comes from Unreal, 3ds Max or Substance in DirectX: its green is flipped. If the relief looks dug in instead of raised, change this setting. Opacity 1: opaque. Lower, you see through it (a window: 0.3); reflections remain. Applies to the materials of a model replaced one by one (below). Emitted light Its color and strength: 0 nothing, higher the surface glows by itself (screens, lamps, lava). Glow at night The glow goes out during the day and switches on at dusk: a sign, a street lamp head. Glow image Its colors: the emitted-light image glows with its own colors. Mask: red, green, blue or alpha: only that channel counts, tinted by the emitted-light color. Unreal vehicles store one group of lights per channel this way (brake, position, indicators): a red tail light, lit only at night with Glow at night. Opening hours of the glow The glow is on only between Opening and Closing, at the hour of the realistic sky (always without it); a range can go past midnight. Shader A surface that moves or glows by itself: a hologram, a dissolve, lava, wind in the leaves. Choose a recipe, tune its sliders: see Shaders. Images Color, relief (normal map), roughness, metal, shadow of hollows, height, emitted light: the path of an image of the project, or drag one from the explorer.

Each setting is undone with Ctrl+Z. The material file is written when you save (and before the game starts).

items.title: Tiled textures (UDIM)
items.text:
Some models (vehicles, detailed characters, exports from Unreal, Maya or Mari) have images cut into UDIM tiles: one file per square of coordinates, car_C.1001.png, car_C.1002.png, car_C.1011.png... To use them, copy all the tiles into the project and write <UDIM> instead of the number in the image path: textures/car_C.<UDIM>.png. This works for every image of the material (color, relief, roughness, metal, shadow of hollows, emitted light).

  • WorldMint assembles the tiles into a single image, laid out like their grid; each one is shrunk so the whole fits in 2048 × 2048 pixels (16 MB per image), the budget of the Medium quality. Only tiles up to the last one the model covers count: empty tiles shipped further away take no room.
  • Each tile keeps a small margin where its edge pixels repeat: filtering never mixes two neighboring tiles (without it, black lines would appear along panels).
  • An empty tile of the color image (transparent and black: nothing is painted there, often the car body) takes the material's Color: it is the paint color, adjustable. The other tiles keep their image, untinted.
  • Roughness, metal and shadow of hollows stored in one image (AO, roughness, metal: red, green, blue): pick the same image for all three, each with its channel.
  • A model made for tiles has coordinates beyond 0-1: with a single ordinary image, it looks badly textured.

items.title: One material per material slot of the model
items.text:
A model exported without its images (from Unreal, for example) often keeps its material slots: names, one per part (body, windows, trim). A file placed next to the model, <model>.materials.json (car.fbx.materials.json), gives each one its project material; * applies to the others:

{"formatVersion": 1, "slots": {"MI_Car_7": "materials/paint.wmmat", "*": "materials/trim.wmmat"}}

The paint then goes on the body only, the window gets a material with a low Opacity, and every object using this model benefits. Paths are counted from the project root.

By hand, without writing the file: select an object made of the model; in Properties, the collapsible Model materials section lists its slots (with the UDIM tiles they cover) and, for each, the list of project materials. The model's own gives it back its own material; All the others stands for *. The .materials.json file is written at once, the model reloads, and Ctrl+Z goes back to the previous choice. Changing one of these materials afterwards also reloads the model. Slot names can also be read with the agent or the asset_probe --details tool.

The exported game carries the .materials.json file, the materials it cites and their images (every UDIM tile), at the same place relative to each other. The model must be inside the project.

items.title: Ground materials
items.text:
A terrain first shows the colors of its regions. Select the Terrain object: the Ground materials section offers Cover with materials. Each region then gets a real material (grass for plains and forests, rock, snow, sand for deserts and beaches, mud for swamps), and three automatic rules are added:

Rule Where it lays its material Slope On ground steeper than an angle (rock on cliffs). Altitude Above a height (snow on peaks). Water's edge Within a distance of water (sand on beaches).

Each rule has its material, its threshold and its Transition (the width of the fade, which waves so as not to draw a line). They apply in order: the last one wins. A switch turns each off.

  • Add: one more material to paint (16 at most). The cross removes it; its painting is erased.
  • Ground material, in the properties of a region: the material that covers it.
  • Variation: slightly lighter or darker areas, and the pattern blended with a larger copy of itself; the repetition of the images no longer shows.
  • Back to the region colors: the ground takes back its colors (Ctrl+Z to return).

On cliffs, the images are laid on the three axes: rock does not stretch. Where two materials blend, the one with the higher relief wins: pebbles stand out of the sand instead of a plain fade.

items.title: The Materials brush
items.text:
In the tool column of the view, Materials paints a material on the ground, over the one of the regions and the rules: hand painting always wins.

Setting Effect Size The radius of the brush, in meters. Strength How fast it covers. Softness 0: a sharp edge. 1: a fade from the center to the edge. The small circle shows where it covers fully. Material The one you paint, among those of the ground. Eraser Erases the painting: the ground takes back the material of its region and of the rules.

Each brush stroke is undone with Ctrl+Z. The painting is stored in tiles of 64 m: a stroke only touches the tiles it covers.

Regions still decide the vegetation, the footsteps and the systems: materials only change the look of the ground.

items.title: With the agent
items.text: The agent can make the same gestures: list, create and put materials, cover the ground, set the rules, paint an area (a square, a field), along a line (a path) or in dabs, erase, then check what covers the ground at a point and look at the result in an image. Each gesture is undone with Ctrl+Z.

items.title: Creating a move
items.text:
A model doesn't always have the move you need: a wolf without a walk, a guard who doesn't wave, a missing attack. Create it in the tool: keyframes bone by bone in the timeline, played in a loop, saved as a move of the model. Systems, timelines and scripts then play it like the moves of the files.

Nothing is specific to a model pack: the skeleton is read from the model, and angles are given around the character's axes, as when adjusting a pose.

items.title: Creating a move
items.text:
1. Select the character in the scene (the player, a guard, an animal: any model with a skeleton).
  2. In its Properties, open Skeleton pose and click Create a move.
  3. Give it a name ("Walk", "Wave"), a length, say whether it is Looping, and choose what it starts from:
    • The rest pose: an empty move, to build;
    • An existing move: read as keyframes, ten per second, to correct it without touching the original file;
    • The adjustment layer: its pose becomes the first keyframe.
  4. The timeline opens at the bottom, on this move: one row per animated bone, grouped by body part (head, back and hips, arms, legs, other bones), each keyframe a diamond.

items.title: Setting keyframes
items.text:
1. Place the playhead: click or drag on the ruler of seconds, or click on a row.
  2. Click a bone, in the view, in the list of bones or on its row in the timeline.
  3. Turn it with the gizmo (E), or move its point (W): the hips move, a hand or a foot bends the arm or the leg, the head or the back lean. Or type its angles under Bone rotation (and, for the hips, Bone offset). With Auto keyframe (on at first), a keyframe is set at the playhead.
  4. Do it again at another moment. Space (the mouse over the timeline) plays the move in a loop.

Every gesture is undone with Ctrl+Z, even on several keyframes at once (with the mouse over the timeline, Delete, Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V and Ctrl+A go to the keyframes, not to the objects of the scene).

Gesture What it does Click a diamond Chooses this keyframe. On the row of a body part or on "All keyframes", all its bones at that moment. Ctrl+click, Shift+click, rectangle As in File Explorer: Ctrl+click adds or removes a keyframe from the choice, Shift+click chooses everything since the last click on this row, a rectangle dragged in empty space chooses what it covers (with Ctrl or Shift, in addition). Ctrl+A chooses them all, Escape none. Drag a diamond Moves all the chosen keyframes in time, together, by the same amount. Right-click a row Keyframe here, Remove keyframes, Copy keyframes, Paste keyframes here, Interpolation, Copy the pose, Paste the pose. Delete Removes the chosen keyframes. Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V Copies the chosen keyframes, then pastes them at the playhead with their spacing (into another move too). Interpolation For the chosen keyframes: linear (steady), smooth (slow at start and end), stepped (it jumps from one pose to the next). Ctrl+wheel, Shift+wheel, Show all Zooms around the mouse, scrolls (or drag the bar under the tracks), then goes back to the whole length. Keyframe Sets a keyframe of the chosen bone at the playhead, or of every animated bone if none is chosen. Copy the pose, Paste the pose Copies the angles of every bone to another moment (the end of a step takes back its start). Copy the left onto the right (or the reverse) The right side takes the left side's pose at that moment, seen in a mirror. Mirror The bone on the other side follows each gesture, as in a mirror. Close the loop Copies the first pose to the end. When looping, a bone with a keyframe at the start already goes back to it at the end. Onion skin Shows the skeleton a little before and a little after, in pale lines. Feet on the ground Turning the hips or the back leaves the feet where they are: the legs bend by themselves (to crouch, to lean). Bone gizmo Turn (E) rotates the bone; Move (W) takes its point where you drag it (the Move and Rotate buttons of the toolbar do the same). A hand or a foot bends the two bones above it. What moves With Move (W): The point alone (key 1, a position keyframe on that bone: nothing else turns), The bone above (key 2, a rotation keyframe on the bone carrying it) or The whole limb (key 3, as below). Bend direction For a moved hand or foot: the elbow or knee bends as in the model's rest pose, otherwise the elbow backward and the knee forward; Forward or Backward force it. Move length, Looping, Move name Can be changed at any time. The same name as a move of the file replaces it everywhere.

Angles are given around the character's axes at rest (as for a pose adjustment): for a model facing forward, X raises a leg or an arm forward (negative angle) or backward, Y turns the bone on itself, Z tilts it sideways.

items.title: Example: a walk for a wolf
items.text:
A walk cycle needs only a few keyframes. For a four-legged animal, at a trot, the legs go in diagonal pairs:

  1. Create "Wolf walk", 1 second, in a loop, from the rest pose.
  2. At 0 s: the front left and back right legs forward (negative X), the other two backward.
  3. At 0.5 s: the reverse (copy the pose of 0 s, paste it, then copy left onto right).
  4. At 0.25 s and 0.75 s: bend the lower part of the leg coming back forward, so it leaves the ground.
  5. Play it in a loop, tune it, then give "Wolf walk" to a system's animation setting (an enemy on patrol), or play it from a script: game.play(id, "Wolf walk").

items.title: Where the move goes
items.text:
It is a file of the project, animations/<name>.wmanim, saved with it. It belongs to the model: every character using this model has it, like the moves of its file (the player in its animation graph, characters through their systems, timelines, scripts). An exported game takes it along. On another model, add it to the player's animation files: it is borrowed like a file, through the bone map.

Pose layers are added on top of this move too, in the game.

items.title: If the model moves
items.text:
The move and the pose adjustments follow the path of their model, and an adjustment follows the name of the move it targets:

  • Rename or move the model in the library (right-click the project model: Rename, F2, or Move to; or drag it onto a folder): whatever uses it follows, the objects of every scene, its moves, its pose adjustments. Ctrl+Z puts the file back. A .gltf, .obj or .fbx, which keep files next to them, can only be renamed in place.
  • Rename the move (Move name): the pose adjustments that targeted it follow, in the same Ctrl+Z.
  • A link broken outside the editor (the model deleted or moved in File Explorer, a changed animation file): Skeleton pose says so in red, and offers Attach to this model, or Attach to a move for an adjustment.

items.title: With the agent
items.text: Just ask: "make a walk for the wolf". The agent reads the bones (pose_layers_get), creates the move (skeleton_animation_set), reads it back (skeleton_animation_get), looks at it frame by frame (view_capture with animation), in a single step that Ctrl+Z undoes. It never touches the model file.

items.title: Playing with several players
items.text: Your game can be played by several players: one player hosts the game on their PC, their friends join it by its address, and each has their own character. Players see each other move, what moves in the world is the same for everyone, everyone hears the game's sounds, and the group follows the host from one scene to the next.

items.title: Three things to remember
items.text:
1. The game is played on the host's computer. The others see and hear what it sends them.
  2. Each player has their own character, interface and controls. A copy of the player's character, with its animations, that walks, runs, jumps, swims, drives and aims like it, with their own health, bag and menus.
  3. A single-player game doesn't change. As long as the setting is off, nothing is different.

items.title: Turning it on
items.text:
With nothing selected, in the game properties, open Multiplayer and tick Several players. These settings appear:

Setting What it does Default Players at most How many players in a game, the host included (2 to 16). With 16 players, the host needs a good connection (fiber) 4 Network port The "door" number through which the others arrive. Change it only if it is already taken 48600 Updates per second How many times per second the host sends each player what moves 20 Each player's range How far each player receives what happens around them; beyond it, they do not see the other players, and what moved far from them is hidden until they come closer. 0: everything, everywhere 250 m Bandwidth per player The most the host sends each player; what is near goes first. 0: no limit 128 kbit/s

You can also ask the agent: "my game is played by four".

items.title: Trying it in the editor
items.text: In Game ▸ Play with several players (or the button of the same name, in the game settings, Multiplayer section), the editor starts the game twice on this PC: one window hosts the game, the other joins it as a friend. You try both sides this way, without exporting or typing an address. Stop closes both.

items.title: Playing with friends
items.text:
In the game, the Menu (the catalog's system) has two more buttons, on the title screen and in the pause:

  • Host a game: the game becomes an online game. The pause then says how many friends are there, and lets you stop it.
  • Join a game: three tabs.
  • List: the public servers of this game (same version), with their players and a lock if they have a password. Click one.
  • Code: the short code the host received (for example K7P-2QMX); the host sees it in the pause.
  • Address: the address of the hosting PC (for example 192.168.1.20), then Join. It always works, even without Internet.
  • A locked server, or one that answers "password missing or wrong", opens a Password field.
  • If it fails (game full, another version of the game, nobody answers), the menu says so.

The list and the codes go through WorldMint's lobby, a service shared by every game (ADR-037 § 4); a game can also use its own: see Hosting your own lobby. If it does not answer, the List and Code tabs say so, and the address is enough. The Menu setting "Short code for the hosted game" (on) gives the host's game a code; "Hosted game in the public list" (off) shows it to everyone. A dedicated server sets it in serveur.json: "public": true and "code_court": true.

It also works from a command prompt: MyGame.exe --heberger (with --code or --public), MyGame.exe --rejoindre 192.168.1.20 --nom Lea, or MyGame.exe --rejoindre-code K7P-2QMX.

Each friend has a key of their own, and the first time they come, the host hands them a secret token, kept on both PCs. When the host resumes a saved game, the friend who comes back with their token finds their bag, health, quests and place again. Someone who took their key without their token arrives as a new player: they get nothing back.

On the host's first start, Windows may ask to allow the game on the network: that is normal. To play over the Internet without changing anything on one's router, the matchmaking service planned later will be needed; until then, the local network works right away.

items.title: What each player sees
items.text:
• Their own character moves right away, without waiting for the host's answer: if the host saw something else (a wall, another player blocking the way), the character is gently put back in place.
  • The other players are shown a tenth of a second in the past, so they glide smoothly even if a message is lost. A pose adjustment that a script switches on or off on a player (game.pose_layer) shows for everyone, on that player.
  • Objects that the rules or physics move, show, hide or destroy change for everyone, like what a player builds, and an object that bursts bursts for everyone.
  • Their own interface: their health, bag, needs and menus. Online, a menu does not stop the game: it only holds the one who opens it.

items.title: Changing scenes, ending the game, sounds
items.text:
• The group follows the host: when the host goes to another scene (a door, a passage), the friends arrive there with them, around them, with their bag and health. If the host starts over, they start over too.
  • The end of the game (won or lost) shows for everyone. The host is the one who plays again.
  • Sounds: what happens in the world (footsteps, hits, the music) is heard by everyone, each from where they stand; the sounds of a player's interface (a click in their menu) are only heard by them.

items.title: Rules and scripts
items.text:
The game's rules only run on the host. A script there sees every player with game.players(), and receives "joueur.arrivee" when a friend arrives and "joueur.depart" when they leave.

A rule that says "the player" must say which one: the one who touched, the nearest, or all. The catalog's systems already do: what a player owns or feels (their health, bag, hunger, quests) is theirs; what is in the world (the time of day, trees, buildings, enemies) is everyone's. A script written for each player carries the line -- multijoueur: par_joueur: it then runs once per player.

items.title: What doesn't work yet
items.text:
• Videos and particles started by the rules are only seen on the host.
  • Players join by the host PC's address: no code to share yet, and no game found by itself on the local network.

items.title: Security
items.text: A game that receives messages from other PCs protects itself: each message is checked (its size, its numbers, the player's name) and refused at the slightest mismatch; a message never carries a script or a file. The host refuses a friend with another version of the game or a game already full, and closes the connection of a friend who sends damaged messages or far too many messages. Exchanges are encrypted. The editor itself never receives anything from the network.

items.title: Physics, zones and character walking
items.text: Two game systems bring objects to life without a script: Physics, for what falls, rolls and gets pushed, and Zone, to know who enters a place. The engine runs them itself; they are set in the Properties, and the agent can place them for you.

items.title: Physics: objects that move
items.text:
Objects that carry the Physics system fall, roll, slide, bounce, and the player pushes them by walking into them, as characters do: crates, barrels, a ball, rocks, a cart.

  1. Activate the system: the Developer mode's Systems panel, Activate under Physics (see The game's systems and settings).
  2. Place it on each object that must move: drag Physics from the library's Systems folder, or + System in the object's Properties. Placed on a folder, it applies to everything the folder contains: each object in the folder moves.
  3. Set the objects on the ground or on each other (Place on ground, End key). An object left in the air falls when the game starts.

An object carrying the system needs no other setting to collide with the others: its shape surrounds its model.

items.title: The settings of each object
items.text:
In the object's Properties, Systems section, under Physics:
