Setting What it does Shape Box: a crate, furniture, Ball: a ball, a round rock or Cylinder: a barrel, a column. A barrel lying on its side rolls if it is a cylinder. Mass (kg): the heavier, the harder to push As a guide: a crate 10 to 30, a barrel 40, a rock 200. Friction: 0 slides as on ice 0.6 at first. Bounce: 0 does not bounce, 1 bounces without losing anything 0.1 at first. In water Floats (half sunk), In between (stays where it is let go), Sinks, or By its density: less than water (1,000 kg per m³), it floats, the higher the lighter it is (cork 200, wood 500); more, it sinks (stone 2,500). Drag in water (1 ordinary) How much the water slows it down and carries it: 0 glides without being held, 3 sticks to the water like a dead leaf.

items.title: The setting for the whole game
items.text: In the Systems panel, Physics card: Force with which the player and characters push (N), 300 at first. At 0, nobody pushes anything.

items.title: Good to know
items.text:
• An object that falls out of the world disappears.
  • In the water of a lake or the sea, it floats or sinks by its In water setting, rocks with the waves and drifts with the water; broken, its pieces too. See What floats.
  • The number of objects physics can follow is a game setting: Max physics bodies, in the technical settings.
  • To throw an object without a script, the Trigger has the action Push a moving object (Physics system).
  • All the settings: the Physics system reference.

items.title: Zones
items.text: A zone announces who enters it and who leaves it: a pressure plate, a trap, a finish line, a goal. It is a box, invisible in the game, that carries the Zone system. The game then decides what happens, most often with the Trigger.

items.title: Creating a zone
items.text:
Object > Create > Zone, or, in the Scene tab, a right-click in the empty space under the list (or Create inside on an object). The zone is a box 2 metres wide, created where you are looking, and set on the ground if the Place on ground when adding preference is on (it is at first). If the Zone system was not activated yet, it is activated at the same time: a single Ctrl+Z removes the zone and the system.

Place it, then give it its size with its Scale: a plate at 2 × 0.2 × 2, a finish line at 10 × 4 × 1. The editor always shows it; in the game, it cannot be seen, and stops nobody.

The Zone system can also go on an ordinary object, a visible slab for example: the zone is then the box of its model, at its place, with its rotation and size.

items.title: Who triggers it
items.text:
In the zone's Properties, Systems section, under Zone, the Who triggers it setting:

Choice Who counts The player The player only (at first). The player and characters The player, and the game's characters (enemies, for example). Moving objects (Physics system) Objects carrying the Physics system: a ball in a goal, a crate on a plate. Everything that moves All of these at once.

What is already in the zone when the game starts enters it at the first moment.

items.title: Making the game react
items.text:
Place the Trigger on the zone, with a When rule: Someone enters this zone (Zone system) (or leaves). A few ideas:

  • A plate that opens a door: Then: Hide an object, the door. The full example is in The Trigger.
  • A trap: a zone at the bottom of a ravine, Then: Teleport the player to an object, a marker on the edge.
  • A finish line: Then: End the game, Victory.
  • A goal: a ball carrying Physics (Shape: Ball: a ball, a round rock), a zone in the net, set to Moving objects (Physics system), and Then: Show a message, "Goal!".

A zone is switched off and back on with the Trigger's Make passable (or switch a zone off) and Make solid (or switch a zone back on) actions: a plate that only works once, a trap disarmed by a lever.

For a richer reaction, the agent can write a script that listens to the zone.entree and zone.sortie events: see the events and the Zone system reference.

items.title: Where characters walk
items.text: Enemies and the other characters that move on their own (the Enemies system, or a script that makes them walk with game.walk_to) follow the walkable areas: the ground a character can reach. They follow the terrain's relief and the top of objects, go around walls, under bridges and up gentle slopes.

items.title: Seeing them
items.text:
View menu, Walkable areas: the scene gets colored over the ground.

Color What it is Blue Where a character can go, starting from the player's place. Orange An isolated spot, where one can stand but that can't be reached from the player: a roof, a room without a door, an island. No color Nobody walks there: a slope too steep, a passage too narrow, water too deep, the inside of an obstacle.

It updates by itself, in the background, when the scene changes: the editor stays usable meanwhile. The world is cut into plots of 32 m, and only those that changed are computed again: moving a house only redoes the plots around it. The console says how many plots were redone, and how long it took.

items.title: What blocks, what doesn't
items.text:
• Blocks: objects with a Collision, the trunks of the terrain's plants (the Trunk setting of their kind of plant), slopes too steep and water deeper than half a character's height.
  • Doesn't block: objects without collision, those with the Physics system (they get pushed), and anything lower than the highest step (a stair, a curb).
  • An object placed high, like a bridge, doesn't block those who walk under it if it leaves enough room.
  • In the game, an obstacle that moves, disappears or becomes passable (a door that opens) redoes the plots it touches: characters get through at once.

items.title: The typical character
items.text: The areas are computed for a typical character, set in the game settings (nothing selected, Character walking section, folded at first): its Radius (half its width; 0.4 m at first), its Height (1.8 m), the Steepest slope it climbs (50°) and the Highest step it steps over (0.35 m). A passage must be wider than twice the radius: a 1 m door lets a 0.4 m-radius character through.

items.title: Several character sizes
items.text:
A rat and a giant don't go through the same doors. In the same section, Add a character size creates another size, with its Name (Small, Large...), its Radius, its Height and its Step: each size has its own walkable areas. Each character takes the smallest size it fits in, from the radius and height its script gives it: a big monster doesn't go into a small one's corridor, and says "blocked" if it has no other way. The slope is the same for all of them. Each size is computed separately: add one only for characters really smaller or larger than the typical one.

View menu, Walkable areas of the size: chooses the size whose areas are shown.

items.title: Characters avoid each other
items.text:
Characters that walk on their own see each other, the player and the other characters coming, and step aside in time: two guards crossing in a corridor walk past each other instead of getting stuck face to face. It is set in the same section:

Setting What it does Characters avoid each other On at first. Off, they bump into and push each other. Avoidance quality How many directions each one tries before choosing. Medium at first; Low for crowds of several hundred. Anticipation How far ahead in time a character sees an encounter coming (2.5 s at first). Longer: it steps aside earlier and more calmly.

items.title: Good to know
items.text:
• A character that finds no path stops ("blocked" for scripts) and tries again every second: a door opened in the meantime lets it through.
  • After a windowless test run of the game, the agent knows which character didn't find its way, and why: placed off the walkable areas, an unreachable target, or no way between them. Its scene check also reports a character placed off the walkable areas, or on an isolated spot the player can't reach.
  • The areas are computed in the editor, not when the game starts. Once the scene is saved, the editor computes the areas of each size in the background, even when they aren't shown, and stores them in the project's work folder (.worldmint), in 256 m pieces: the game reads them back when it starts instead of computing them again. After a change, only the changed plots are redone. The exported game takes these areas along. It only computes what is missing (a scene never saved, a project just copied): about one second for a 512 m map on an eight-core computer, several seconds for a map of several kilometres.

items.title: Asking the agent
items.text:
• "Make these crates and barrels pushable."
  • "Put a ball in the middle of the field, and a goal: when the ball goes into the goal, show "Goal!"."
  • "Add a plate in front of the door: when the player steps on it, the door opens."

After running the game without a window, the agent can tell how far each moving object travelled, and whether it fell out of the world.

items.title: Adjusting a character's pose
items.text:
A move is often almost right: on the motorbike, the hands don't quite land on the handlebar; an arm goes through the body; a guard stands too straight. Rather than looking for another animation file, adjust the pose: turn a few bones, and the adjustment is added to the move, wherever it plays in the game.

Nothing is specific to a model pack: the skeleton is read from the model, its bones are recognised by their name and by its shape, and angles are given around the character's axes, not each bone's own.

items.title: Adjusting a pose
items.text:
1. Select the character in the scene (the player, a guard, an animal: any model with a skeleton).
  2. In its Properties, open Skeleton pose and click Adjust the pose. Its skeleton appears in the view: one point per bone, and the list of bones below.
  3. Choose the preview: the rest pose, one of its moves (playing, or stopped at a moment with the slider), or Seated on a motorbike / Seated in a car for the pose the game gives the driver.
  4. Click a bone, in the view or in the list (its plain name is in brackets: Left hand, Back…).
  5. Turn it with the gizmo (E, or Turn under Bone gizmo), or type its three angles under Bone rotation. The character changes before your eyes.
  6. Or move its point (W, or Move): drag it where it should be. What moves chooses what follows it: The point alone (the default, key 1) moves only it, with what it carries, without turning anything above (the bone above stretches or shortens); The bone above (key 2) only turns the bone carrying it, without stretching it; The whole limb (key 3) does what follows. The hips really move (to crouch, to lean); a hand or a foot bends the two bones above it without stretching them, the elbow backward and the knee forward (Bend direction for the other way); a foot keeps its orientation, flat; an elbow, a knee, the head or the back turn the bones that carry them. The layer still stores angles (and the hips' offset).

Every gesture is undone with Ctrl+Z.

Setting What it does Adjustment layer A layer groups turned bones. The first adjustment creates one, for the move shown. A model can have several. Adjusted move One move, Every move, or Seated on a vehicle (the driver's pose). Adjustment strength From 0 to 100% of the angle. Layer on Off, it no longer plays: handy to compare before and after. Mirror The bone on the other side follows, as in a mirror. Copy the left onto the right (or the reverse) The right side takes the left side's adjustments, mirrored. Reset the bone, Reset everything Removes the adjustment of one bone, or of the whole layer. Copy the pose, Paste the pose Copies the angles into another layer or onto another character; bones it does not have are ignored.

Angles are given around the standing character's axes: X tilts the bone forward or back, Y turns it around, Z tilts it sideways. Small angles (5 to 30°) are usually enough.

items.title: Example: hands on the handlebar
items.text:
A motorbike rider takes a pose the game builds from the skeleton (Vehicles). To correct it:

  1. Select the player's character, Adjust the pose, preview Seated on a motorbike.
  2. Click the left upper arm, switch Mirror on, and turn it forward: both hands move towards the handlebar.
  3. Click the back and lean it slightly forward.

In the game, every time they get on a vehicle, they take this pose.

items.title: Creating a skeleton
items.text:
A model without a skeleton (a statue, an animal imported without bones, a free model, a model made by an AI) cannot be animated. Create a skeleton for it:

  1. Pick the model in the scene, then open Skeleton pose.
  2. Choose a Template:
    • Biped: a standing character, arms spread (hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, shoulders, arms, legs). The tool measures where its limbs bend: the shoulder where the arm enters the body, the wrist where the arm narrows before the hand, the elbow between them, the ankle where the foot ends, the knee halfway down the leg, the head at the narrowest point of the neck;
    • Quadruped: a four-legged animal (hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, four legs of 3 or 4 bones, a tail chain; the Ears are optional);
    • Simple chain: a tail, a tentacle, a plant (choose the Number of bones);
    • Single bone: a whole object that moves, such as a door or a chest (put the joint on the hinge).
  3. Click Create a skeleton. The template is fitted to the model: the editor measures its shape (front and back, leg height, where the feet, the head and the tail are, and an open mouth). The skeleton shows inside the model, in Correct the skeleton mode.
  4. Move the misplaced joints, as when correcting a skeleton: Move (W), Turn (E), Remove this joint, Add a joint here. Until the skin is attached, the whole model follows the root.
  5. Click Attach the skin: the editor works out how every part of the model follows every bone. Run it again after moving joints.

The skin follows the model's volume, not a straight line: the upper teeth do not follow the lower jaw across an open mouth, and a leg does not take the skin of the next one. Joints bend smoothly.

Skin softness sets how wide the passage from one bone to the next is: higher, the skin bends over a longer stretch, without folds or creases; 0 gives sharp passages. When you release the slider, the skin is worked out again in the background. The Quadruped template gives five bones to the back (from the hips to the chest) and two or three to the neck, placed from the model's shape: the back curves when galloping, the neck turns smoothly. A skeleton created before keeps its bones: create it again to get this template.

items.title: The skin method
items.text:
For every animated model (its own skeleton or a created one), Skin method, at the top of Correct the skeleton, says how the skin follows the bones at the joints:

  • Preserve volume: a bent knee, elbow or neck keeps its thickness, and a bone turned on itself does not twist the skin like a candy wrapper;
  • Linear: the classic blend of most engines, where the skin pinches at the folds;
  • Automatic (the default): preserve volume.

The choice is saved with the project, for this model, and applies everywhere: the editor, the game, shadows and ray tracing.

If the measure is wrong (the head taken for the tail, a model lying down), switch on Swap front and back or choose the Model's up, before creating the skeleton or in Create the skeleton again. The skin is worked out in the background, with a progress bar: you can keep working. It is then stored in the project and not worked out again when loading.

The bones have common names (Hips, Spine, Head, Jaw, LeftArm, LeftUpLeg, Tail...): the model can then borrow the moves of another skeleton, including those of another four-legged animal whose bones are named differently (legs, spine, head and tail are found from the skeleton's shape), and you can create its moves in the timeline. A biped directly plays the human animations of the library (Animations folder, Give to the characters), and those of the standard skeletons of packs (Unreal or Mixamo names).

Like a correction, the created skeleton is saved with the project, for this model: the model file is never changed. It applies wherever the model plays (the editor, the game, an exported game, multiplayer) and follows the model when you rename or move it. Remove the created skeleton takes it away; Ctrl+Z undoes each step.

items.title: Correcting the skeleton
items.text:
Many models have a badly placed skeleton, above all when it was rigged automatically (a model made by an AI, a skeleton added in one click): a knee behind the leg, an elbow inside the arm. The limb then bends beside the place where it should bend. Rather than adjusting each move, correct the skeleton itself:

  1. In Skeleton pose, click Adjust the pose, then switch on Correct the skeleton. The character shows at rest, its skeleton on top.
  2. Click the misplaced joint, in the view or in the bone list.
  3. Move (W): drag the joint where the limb should bend. Turn (E): turn it on itself, if the limb bends sideways. The model does not move: only the joint's place inside it changes. Ctrl+Z undoes the gesture.
  4. Switch Correct the skeleton off and pick a move in the preview: the limb now bends around the new joint, in every move of the model (those of its file, those you made, those borrowed from another character, and the adjustments).

By default, the joints below the one you move follow it (moving the shoulder takes the arm along). Switch on Move the joint alone to leave them where they are. The Joint offset and Joint rotation fields give the same settings as numbers.

  • Remove this joint: the skin it moved follows its parent, and the joints it carried are attached to the parent, at the same place. Its animations are ignored. The root of the skeleton cannot be removed. Restore the joint brings it back.
  • Add a joint here: a new joint, child of the chosen one, that you name and then place with the gizmo. Without skin it is an attach point: a weapon, a held object (Held by the character), particles. With Take the skin around, it takes from its parent the part of the model beyond it, with a smooth transition: it then bends that part, like the tip of a tail. It can then be animated like the other joints (adjustments, moves, timeline).
  • Reset this joint and Back to the original skeleton undo one correction or all of them.

The correction is saved with the project, for this model: the model file is never changed. It applies wherever the model plays: in the editor, in the game, in an exported game and for the other players in multiplayer. It follows the model when you rename or move it in the library. If the model was moved outside the editor, Skeleton pose shows it in red: Attach to this model gives it back to the chosen model.

items.title: Where adjustments go
items.text:
They belong to the model and are saved with the project: every character using this model has them (the player, script characters, other players in multiplayer). The model file is never modified.

A script can switch a layer on, off or partly for a single character: game.pose_layer(id, "Hunched guard", 0.5) (see the scripts reference). In multiplayer, what it changes on a player shows for everyone.

Renaming or moving the model in the library, or renaming the adjusted move, makes the adjustments follow; a link broken outside the editor is attached again in Skeleton pose (see Creating a move).

items.title: With the agent
items.text:
Just ask: "on the motorbike, move his hands a bit forward onto the handlebar and lean his back". The agent reads the skeleton and the layers (pose_layers_get), then changes them (pose_layers_set), in a single step that Ctrl+Z undoes. It never touches the model file.

For a badly placed skeleton: "the wolf's left knee is too far back, bring it to the middle of the leg". The agent reads the skeleton at rest (skeleton_fix_get), then corrects it (skeleton_fix_set: move, turn, remove or add a joint), also in a single Ctrl+Z.

For a model without a skeleton: "create a quadruped skeleton for this wolf, then attach the skin". The agent creates the skeleton (skeleton_create), checks its joints (skeleton_fix_get, then a capture where it bends a leg), moves the misplaced ones (skeleton_fix_set), then attaches the skin (skeleton_bind).

items.title: A project
items.text:
A project is a folder that holds your whole game. It can be moved, copied, sent or backed up like any folder, without repairing anything:

My game/
  My game.worldmint    the project file: the whole game and its start scene
  scenes/              the scenes (.wmscene)
  assets/              the models, sounds and images the game uses, copied from your library
  AGENT.md             optional: the agent's rules for this project
  .worldmint/          working files: the conversation with the agent, automatic backups, deleted scenes
  • Create: File > New project.... The creation assistant then offers its help.
  • Open: File > Open project..., then the .worldmint file.
  • Find it in File Explorer: File > Open project folder.
  • A scene outside a project (an old file): File > Create a project from this scene... makes it a project, copying its models into it. The original scene is not touched.

When you use a model from the library, its file (and those it names, like its textures) is copied into assets/. A file already in the project is never overwritten: changing the library does not change the project.

A project made by a newer version of the editor does not open: update the editor.

items.title: The whole game and each scene
items.text:
A game can have several places: the outdoors, the inside of a house, a cave, levels that follow each other. Each place is a scene. Some things apply to the whole game, others to each scene:

The whole game Each scene The played character: its model, animations, settings Its objects, terrain, vegetation, water Activated systems and their settings for the whole game The systems placed on its objects, with their values The game's scripts Its light and sky Controls, window, simulation Its placed cameras, and the one that opens it Reusable objects Its arrival points The start scene

Scripts keep running when the player changes scene, and keep their variables.

items.title: Managing scenes
items.text:
In the Scene tab, the Game scenes section (see The Scene tab):

  • + creates a new scene;
  • a click opens a scene (the editor first offers to save the open one);
  • right-click: Open, Rename, Duplicate, Delete, Start the game here.

The word Start marks the scene where the game starts. F5 always plays from the scene you are looking at, to try it; the exported game starts on the start scene.

A scene name cannot contain < > : " / \ | ? *, nor start or end with a dot or a space, and has 80 characters at most.

items.title: Linking scenes
items.text:
To have a door lead inside a house:

  1. In the house's scene, create an arrival point (Object > Create > Arrival point, or right-click in the list): this is where the player will appear, facing the arrow. Name it (for example "Entrance").
  2. In the start scene, activate the Passage system (Systems panel), and place it on the door.
  3. In the door's properties, Systems section, choose the Scene it leads to, then the Arrival: an arrival point of that scene.

The scene list then shows next to the door → House · Entrance, in red if the scene or the arrival does not exist. An arrival point's properties list the passages that lead to it. The player takes the passage with the interaction key (E by default), or by walking into it if Taken by walking into it, without a key is checked: see the Passage system. Think of the way back: a passage in the house, leading to an arrival point in front of the door. The player keeps everything when changing scene (inventory, health...).

A script can also change scene with game.go_to: see the scripts reference.

Before playing, if the scene you start has neither the player's character nor an arrival point, the editor warns you ("An arrival point is missing"): the player would appear anywhere. Create an arrival point places one where you are looking; Play anyway starts the game.

items.title: Saving and recovering
items.text:
• Ctrl+S saves the open scene, and the whole game with it.
  • An automatic backup keeps a separate copy every 60 seconds (set in the Preferences), without touching your files. The status bar shows the time of the last one.
  • If the editor closed without saving, it offers Recover your work? on the next launch. After Recover, save to keep it.
  • A deleted scene is set aside in .worldmint/: nothing is lost.

items.title: Large worlds
items.text:
A map of several kilometers is heavy: saving all of it on every Ctrl+S would take time. The Large world setting (nothing selected, Technical settings section) stores the scene in pieces of 256 m, in files next to it:

scenes/
  Ville.wmscene       the scene: its settings, and the list of its pieces
  Ville.tuiles/       one file per 256 m piece: its objects, its relief, its retouched plants
  • Nothing changes in the editor: you work as before, and you never see the pieces.
  • Only the pieces that changed are rewritten: a moved object or a brush stroke on the relief only saves the piece it touched. Undoing a brush stroke also keeps only the pieces it touched.
  • Nothing is lost if the computer stops while saving: the scene reopens as it was before, or as it is after, never half-way. If a piece is missing or damaged (by an incomplete copy, for example), the scene refuses to open and says which one, without changing anything.
  • Switching to a large world keeps the previous file next to it (Ville.wmscene.avant-grand-monde.bak). Going back (unticking) writes the scene again as a single file and sets the pieces aside (Ville.tuiles.bak).
  • Copying or sending a scene: take the .wmscene file and its .tuiles folder. Renaming, duplicating or deleting a scene from the editor takes them together.
  • Export takes the pieces with the game, and the exported game reads them all.

A small scene does not need this setting: it stays a single file.

To work on one part of the map without seeing the rest, and to lock what is finished, cut it into sectors: see The Scene tab. Sectors are saved with the scene; working on one and saving still rewrites only the pieces that changed.

items.title: What sleeps far from the player
items.text:
In a large world, the game only brings to life what is around the player. Beyond the Activity radius (300 m by default, under Large world), in squares of 256 m, objects fall asleep: they are still there and can be seen, but characters stop walking, moving objects stop, animations and zones wait. When the player comes back, they wake up as the world kept them. The radius is the same on every computer: your game plays the same everywhere.

  • What must live far away (a messenger crossing the map, a boss on patrol): tick Always active in the object's Details, or Objects always active on a system's card, in the Systems panel. Keep it for few objects: what stays awake far away costs at every moment of the game. The editor shows how many there are, under Activity radius and in the object's Details, in red beyond Always active, advised (100 by default); the agent is warned too.
  • Scripts only see what is awake when they look for objects; they can ask for the sleeping ones too, and learn who falls asleep and who wakes up (see the scripts reference, game.awake).
  • A small scene never sleeps: everything stays awake.

items.title: Saved games
items.text: A player who leaves your game can pick it up later, where they were: a key to save, a checkpoint that saves by itself, a game that continues as soon as it starts. Ask the agent ("the player saves with F5 and continues at start"): it has a recipe for this, and sets it up the way you want.

items.title: What a saved game keeps
items.text:
A save has three parts, and you don't have to deal with any of them:

  • the game itself: where the player is and what the game has noted (a lever pulled, a choice made in a dialogue). This is what the agent's recipe stores;
  • the systems: each keeps its own state (see What a saved game keeps): what the player carries in the Inventory, the progress of the Quest log, the Shop stocks, the Dialogue marks;
  • the world: everything the game changed in the scenes, compared to what you placed in the editor.

items.title: The world remembers
items.text:
The engine keeps by itself what changed during the game, and puts it back when loading:

What changed For example An object shown or hidden A secret door that appears, a chest hidden once opened An object solid or not A wall you can walk through after a spell A place, a rotation, a size An object teleported by the Trigger, a crate pushed, a rock that rolled (with its speed: it goes on as it was going) An object destroyed, a copy created A defeated enemy does not come back; arrows stuck in a wall and enemies spawned during the game are still there Tags An object marked "opened" or "visited" by a script Lights A lamp switched on or off, recoloured, made brighter or dimmer (see Light and shadows) The sun and the sky The time of the Day and night system, a storm a script brought (see Making a survival game) Looping effects and decals A fire lit on an object, smoke placed somewhere, a stain on the ground The camera The placed camera that was showing the scene Animations playing A platform going back and forth carries on where it was Trees and plants A tree cut down stays cut down Joints, ragdolls, vehicles A door open, a plank broken, a character on the ground, the car and who drives it The player's settings Slower, unable to run or jump

Only the differences with the placed scene go into the save: it stays small, even for a large world.

items.title: Several scenes
items.text: A game with several places (a cave, the inside of a house) keeps the state of every scene visited, not only the one the player is in. During the game, a scene you leave stays as you left it; after loading too: the cave where the player took a treasure stays empty when they go back, even if they saved outside.

items.title: What a saved game does not keep
items.text:
• The player's exact place is the one the recipe stores; a script of yours can keep more.
  • What only lasts an instant: a sound, a burst of sparks, the pieces of an object that shatters.
  • The exact pose of a character on the ground: they fall again where they were.

items.title: Where the saves are kept
items.text:
• When trying the game in the editor (Play), saves go to the project's work folder (.worldmint/saves), apart from the players'.
  • In the exported game, they go to the player's Windows data, under the game's name: they survive an update of the game.
  • The agent's test runs keep their saves in memory: they never touch a real file.

A save made with an older version of WorldMint can still be read: what it does not contain stays as at the start.

items.title: For scripts
items.text: game.save(slot, table) and game.load(slot) do all of this: the game's table, the systems, the world. {systems = false} as the last argument leaves the systems and the world out, to read a save without resuming it. The scripts reference details these functions.

items.title: Shaders
items.text:
A shader tells the graphics card what a surface looks like. A material sets values (color, roughness, metal, images, glow); a shader goes further: a scrolling hologram, an object that dissolves into embers, flowing lava, a glowing rim, a tree that sways in the wind, cartoon water.

A shader goes on a material: every object that uses this material shows it. It only changes the surface (color, relief, roughness, metal, emitted light, cut-out holes) and, if it wants, where the vertices are. Lighting, shadows, transparency and anti-aliasing stay with the engine: a shader cannot break them.

items.title: Using a recipe
items.text:
Select an object that uses a project material. In the Material section, under Emitted light, the Shader list offers the project's shaders and the Recipes shipped with WorldMint:

Recipe What it does Hologram Scrolling lines and a glowing rim, on an almost black surface. Dissolve The object vanishes in patches, edged with embers; its shadow follows. Wind in foliage The top of the model sways, its foot stays in place (trees, bushes, tall grass). Glowing rim The edge of the object shines, like a magic item or one to pick up. Stylized water Opaque water with bold colors, sparkles and small waves. Lava Dark rock crossed by burning veins that flow slowly. Blinking The surface lights up and goes off, like a warning light.

Choosing a recipe copies it into the project's shaders/ folder: it is now your shader. Its settings appear just below, as sliders (a color, a speed, a strength...). They only change this material: two materials can use the same shader with different colors. Reset the shader's settings gives each one back the value its code gives it.

items.title: Changing the code
items.text:
A shader's code is a small text file, shaders/<name>.wmshader. Two ways to change it:

  • Shader code, in the material panel: type, and the shader is checked and recompiled as soon as you stop. The view shows the result at once.
  • Open the file: it opens in your text editor. Each time you save, WorldMint reads it again and recompiles it.

A shader is written in framed GLSL:

// Hologram: the first line describes the shader.
param color glow = vec3(0.2, 0.8, 1.0);       // a setting: a color swatch
param float speed = 2.0 range(0, 10);         // a slider, from 0 to 10

void surface(inout Surface s, Inputs i) {
    float line = step(0.5, fract(i.position.y * 8.0 - i.time * speed));
    s.color = glow * 0.08;
    s.emission = glow * (fresnel(i.normal, i.toCamera, 3.0) + line * 0.25);
}

void vertex(inout vec3 position, VertexInputs v) {  // optional: moves the vertices
    position.y += 0.05 * sin(v.time * 3.0 + position.x);
}
What the shader changes (Surface s) What it reads (Inputs i) color: the base color, from 0 to 1 position: the point, in the world roughness: 0 smooth, 1 matte normal: the model's normal metallic: 0 or 1 uv: the texture coordinates emission: the emitted light time: game time, in seconds (pauses do not count) opacity: under 0.5, the point vanishes toCamera: the direction of the camera normal: the relief, in the world tint: the object's color

Vertices read local (the vertex in the model), normal, uv and time, and move position (in the world). The library: noise (a soft noise from 0 to 1), fresnel (the edge seen from the front), quality() (0 in Low quality, 1 Medium, 2 High: a costly shader gets simpler in Low), daylight() (the outdoor light, about 1.5 in full daylight and under 0.25 at night: emitted light, like a lit window, fades by day when set against it), hour() (the hour of the sky, 0 to 24; negative without a realistic sky: opening hours), night() (the night share, 0 by day to 1 at night: the same signal as "switches on at night" lights, the street lamps; a window or a sign switches on with it), kelvin(k) (the color of a bulb at k kelvins, luminance 1: 2700 a warm white, 4000 a neutral white; household light is white or yellow, never colored). Eight settings at most: float, vec2, vec3, vec4, or color.

items.title: Connected blocks
items.text:
Without writing code, a shader can be built with connected blocks: each block does one simple thing (read the time, make noise, mix two colors, light up the rim), and you join them like pipes, up to the Output block, which receives what the shader changes: color, emitted light, roughness, metal, opacity, relief, and the vertex displacement. The file is shaders/<name>.wmgraph.

  • Start: in the material's Shader list, choose New shader in blocks, or a recipe in blocks (each of the seven recipes exists in code and in blocks, with the same settings and the same image). Open the blocks opens the Shader blocks window over the bottom of the view: the object stays visible above it, and the material's sphere in the properties.
  • Add a block: the Add a block button, or a right click on the background. Blocks are sorted by family (Inputs, Values and settings, Math, Patterns and effects, Vectors and colors), with a search; hover a block to read what it does.
  • Connect: drag from the dot on the right of a block (its Result) to the dot on the left of another one (one of its inputs). Dropping a link in empty space opens the menu: the block you choose is already connected. A free input takes the small value set next to it.
  • Move, delete: drag a block by its title; its place is saved in the file. Click a block or a link, then Delete. Right-drag to move the background. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo, with the mouse over the window.
  • Settings: a Setting block (a number, with its name, value, minimum and maximum) or Color setting becomes a slider of the material, like a param in code.
  • Preview: each change is checked and compiled 0.3 s later, and the view shows it at once.
  • Show the code shows the code the blocks give, read-only: you change it through the blocks.

A link that does not fit (a loop, two different sizes, a surface block connected to the vertex displacement) is refused: the faulty block turns red, with its message, and the object keeps the last version that worked.

items.title: When the code is refused
items.text:
A shader is checked in three steps before it shows: the text (nothing the engine keeps for itself: no #, no resource, no while, loops of 64 turns at most), a compilation in a "sandbox" that only knows the contract above, then the compilation in the engine's real shader. If one refuses:

  • the panel says why, and on which line ("line 4: writing error, on this line or at the end of the previous one"); so do the console and the status bar;
  • objects keep the last version that worked, or their base material if there is none yet: nothing disappears, nothing turns pink.

After the shader, the engine replaces any value that is not finite (a division by zero) with the material's, and bounds everything else: a wrong shader never makes a black stain or breaks the image.

items.title: With the agent
items.text: The agent knows the recipes and the contract. Ask it "make this chest glow", "have the trees sway in the wind" or "cartoon water for the pond": it puts a recipe on the material and tunes its sliders, or writes a shader, in code or in blocks (it reads and changes the graph you see in the blocks window). It gets the same messages as you, by line, and fixes them before saying it is done. It never changes a shader from a pack: it copies it into shaders/.

items.title: Safety, exported game, performance
items.text:
• A shader from a downloaded pack is recompiled from its text, in a separate process: a booby-trapped text cannot crash the editor.
  • The exported game compiles nothing: the editor stores the compiled versions in the project, and the export takes them along. If a shader is refused, the game draws the material without it.
  • Checking and compiling a shader takes 5 to 7 ms; the graphics card then prepares its pipeline (0.1 to 0.5 s the very first time, a few milliseconds afterwards), on the side: the editor does not freeze, the object keeps the previous version until the new one is ready.

items.title: Sound and the sound mixer
items.text:
A WorldMint game plays WAV, MP3, OGG or FLAC files from your library: footsteps, hits, a fire's crackle, a music. The Sounds system places them on what makes them, without code (see its reference); a script plays them with game.sound and game.music (see the scripts reference).

All these sounds go through the game's sound mixer: it sets the balance between the music, the noises, the ambience and the voices, for the whole game and all its scenes.

items.title: Sound groups
items.text:
Every sound belongs to a group. A new game has five, which always stay:

Group Name for scripts What goes in it Music music the background music, the fight music Effects effects noises: steps, hits, doors, gathering (by default, any sound without a group) Ambience ambience the loops of a place: a fire, a river, the wind Voice voice what characters say Interface ui small cues: a menu click, an item picked up

They are set in the Game settings panel, Sounds section (the Game settings button at the top of the Systems panel):

  • the slider sets the group's volume, from 0 to 100%;
  • the speaker mutes it (it is no longer heard); a second click brings it back;
  • Add a group creates a new one: a radio, a boss's voice. Its name is enough; the name for scripts comes from it ("Radio de bord" gives radio_de_bord), and shows on hover. The cross removes an added group; the five default ones cannot be removed.

Lowering a group changes all its sounds at once: for an ambience that is too loud, lower Ambience rather than each fire.

items.title: Automatic ducking
items.text:
A ducking rule makes a group quieter while another one plays, then brings it back: the music goes under the voices, without a script. A new game has one: Voice lowers Music to 40%.

In the Automatic ducking section:

  • While this group plays: the group that triggers it (a sound too far away to be heard does not count, nor a muted group);
  • Lower this group: the one that gets quieter;
  • Down to: how much of its volume it keeps;
  • Fall time and Recovery time: in how many seconds it gets quieter, then comes back once silence returns.

Add a ducking rule creates another one; Remove this ducking rule deletes it.

items.title: Muffling the sound
items.text:
A muffled group loses its highs, as if heard under water, behind a wall or through a radio. From 0 (clear sound) to 1 (under water).

  • While playing, most often: a Trigger rule with the action Muffle the sound. For example on a zone placed over the water: "on entering", muffle All the game's sound to 1; "on leaving", to 0. The action Mute or unmute a group of sounds silences a group (the ambience during a story scene), then brings it back.
  • All the time: the folded Muffled groups section muffles a group for the whole game.

There is no echo or reverb yet.

items.title: The game window in the background
items.text:
When the player minimizes the game window, or switches to another window (a browser, a chat), the folded section Game window in the background decides what the sound does:

  • Mute the sound (the starting setting): the game goes silent, then comes back when the player returns;
  • Lower the sound: it goes on, quieter (Lowered to, 30% by default);
  • Keep the sound: nothing changes, for a game you listen to while doing something else.

The sound fades out and back in smoothly, without clicks. A game started in the background for a test (by the agent or the tests) always stays silent: you never hear a test you are not watching.

items.title: The player's Options menu
items.text: The Menu system offers the player, in Options, Sound section, the Master volume and one setting per group of the sound mixer, under its name in the player's language. Their choice adds to your mix: if they set the music to 50% and you set it to 80%, it plays at 40%.

items.title: In scripts
items.text:
• game.sound(file, {group = "ambience"}) puts a sound in a group, by its name for scripts or by its name ("Ambience"); without group, it goes to Effects. game.music goes to Music.
  • game.mute(group, true) mutes a group, game.mute(group, false) brings it back; "master" means all the sound.
  • game.muffle(group, 0.8, {fade = 0.5}) muffles it, over half a second.
  • game.volume(group, 0.5) sets the player's volume, for an options menu of your own.
  • game.sound_groups() gives the list of groups, with their name in the player's language.

A group that does not exist is an error, shown in the game's console.

items.title: With the agent
items.text: The agent puts the sounds it writes in the right group, sets the balance with the sound mixer rather than by changing each sound, and places the Trigger rules for the water or a cave. When it tries the game, its report says how many sounds played in each group, and what the scripts muted or muffled.

items.title: Making a survival game
items.text: A survival game is played with what one gathers: chop trees and break rocks, craft tools, build a shelter, eat and drink so as not to die, and nights go by. WorldMint already does each of these parts: ask the agent in your own words, and it assembles the systems and sets them for your game, without any programming.

items.title: The simplest way: the creation assistant
items.text:
In Game > Creation assistant, tick Survival (or Gathering and crafting) in the genre. A Survival step is added:

  • what the character needs to live: eating, drinking, sleeping;
  • crafting items, and which ones: at stations that progress (a workbench one upgrades, a campfire to cook, an oven, a forge);
  • learning recipes before crafting them, and how they are discovered: Like Valheim (discover by picking up), Like Rust (research table), Points tree (like ARK). The first two are ticked by default;
  • building a shelter, and how pieces are placed (on a grid, or freely).

Everything is ticked by default; untick what your game does not want. Days and nights, and how long a whole day lasts (10, 20 or 40 minutes), are asked with the mood (the The mood step), for every game: for a survival or gathering game, the answer is already Yes. At the end, the request sent to the agent names the systems to activate.

items.title: The example progression
items.text:
A new game receives example stations, recipes and knowledges, which you change or delete in the Systems tab (or by asking the agent, in your words). They make a real progression:

Where What is made there How it is learned Bare-handed A stone axe (3 wood, 2 stones) Known from the start Workbench, level 1 A pickaxe, a spear Known from the start (stone tools) Workbench, level 2 (10 wood, 4 stones to upgrade) A bow; an iron axe and pickaxe The bow: by studying a bow found at a research table; iron: by picking up iron ore Workbench, level 3 (20 wood, 5 iron) What you add there Campfire (burns wood) Cooked meat, grilled fish, grilled berries Known from the start (cooking on the fire) Oven (burns wood while cooking) The same, plus bread and stew By obtaining flour Forge (burns wood while working) Iron, smelted from 2 iron ores With the iron tools

The campfire is a cooking station: one cooks there, one does not make tools there. Its window (E) only shows its recipes; what is made bare-handed (the stone axe) is in the crafting window (C). The Crafting setting "At a station, also show the bare-handed recipes" adds them. Any object becomes a station (its "Function": Workbench, Campfire, Oven, Forge…) or a research table, an imported model included. Knowledge can also be learned with points, a plan, a character, a quest: see the Knowledge system.

items.title: The systems
items.text:
System What it does What the player sees Gathering Placed on what can be gathered (a tree, a rock, a bush, a whole plant kind): the number of hits, what it gives, the tool needed (the axe chops wood), and whether it grows back. What needs a tool is struck with the attack, the tool held in hand The prompt "Click: Chop 2/3", then "+3 Wood" Inventory What the player carries, and the bar of items in hand at the bottom of the screen: the axe held shows in the character's hand The bar, the chosen slot, the axe in the hand Crafting The recipes: a "Recipe" row (what it gives) followed by its ingredients. An ingredient can be a tool that is kept (a hammer). A recipe can need a station: an object of the world carrying this system (a workbench one upgrades, a campfire or an oven burning wood, a forge), with its levels, its fuel and its queue The crafting window (C); in front of a station (E), its recipes, its fire and its upgrade Building The pieces: a "Piece" row (its name and its model, a hidden object of the scene) followed by its cost. The piece stands on what is aimed at, measured on its model, whatever it is Building mode (B): a preview where the player aims, blinking where it cannot go. With a character, one aims with the view (the centre of the screen) and the camera keeps turning; from above, with the cursor Needs Hunger, thirst, tiredness, or whatever you want: each goes down over time (faster while running); at zero, the player loses health. Foods of the inventory raise them, as does a source in the world (a well, a bed) or a Trigger rule ("Raise a need"). Each need can be switched off without losing its settings (its "On" box) One bar per need that is on, under the health bar Day and night The sun rises, crosses the sky and sets; night is darker and bluish. Broad daylight is your scene's light as you set it The sky and the light changing; a clock if you want one Knowledge What the player knows how to do: knowledges that unlock recipes, pieces or tags, each learned in one or several ways (from the start, by obtaining an item, by studying an item at a research table, with points, by reading a plan, from a character or a quest, by analysing objects of the world, by crafting again and again). What is not learned stays closed, and the refusal says how to learn it. Any object can become a research table The knowledge window (K): known, to learn, locked, as a tree by category; "Learned: Bow" at the top of the screen

Each one keeps its state in a saved game: the hits already struck and the time before a tree grows back, the pieces built, each need, the day and the time.

items.title: Playing
items.text:
Key (gamepad) What it does 1 to 9, wheel (←, which goes round the slots) Choose what is held in hand, in the bar; the key of the chosen slot puts the item away Click (X) Strike: chop the tree or break the rock, the tool in hand (the axe, the pickaxe) E (Y) Pick bare-handed (berries), use a workbench, drink at a well, sleep in a bed C (left stick pressed) Open or close crafting K Open or close knowledge: spend points; in front of a research table (E), study an item I (Back) The inventory: a click on a food eats or drinks it B (RB) Enter or leave building mode Click (X) Place the piece, where one aims: the centre of the screen with a character, the cursor from above. Fighting does not strike during the mode Wheel (right stick pressed) Turn the piece Q (←), or 1 to 9 Change piece X (B) Tear down the piece aimed at, which gives back part of its cost

All these keys can be changed in the Game controls panel.

items.title: What you can ask the agent
items.text:
• "Trees give 3 wood in 4 axe blows, and grow back after 5 minutes."
  • "An axe is made from 3 wood and 2 stones; meat is cooked at the campfire."
  • "The workbench can be upgraded twice; iron tools need the level 2 workbench."
  • "I build wooden walls and floors, on a grid; a wall costs 4 wood."
  • "I get hungry after 20 minutes and thirsty after 10; an apple raises hunger by 30."
  • "A day lasts 20 minutes; the lanterns light up at night; wolves come out at night."
  • "I sleep in the bed to skip the night."
  • "The bronze axe is discovered by picking up copper, like in Valheim."
  • "A research table, like in Rust: an item destroyed there with scrap teaches how to craft it."
  • "Each level gives 2 points to spend in a tree, like ARK's engrams."
  • "Tiredness also goes back up by drinking a coffee, or resting by the campfire."
  • "Remove tiredness for now": the agent unticks its "On" box, its settings stay.

The agent tells you the numbers it chose (how long each need lasts, what a wall costs, how many hits a tree takes) and checks them by playing: doing nothing does not win, and starving takes minutes, not seconds.

items.title: Good to know
items.text:
• The same names everywhere: an item is one inventory kind, written the same in gathering, recipes, costs and foods ("Wood", not "wood" here and "Wooden plank" there).
  • A piece that does something keeps its model's systems: a campfire carrying Crafting becomes a fire to cook on wherever it is built; a bed carrying Needs lets the player sleep.
  • Tiredness is a row of the Needs like hunger: energy comes back by sleeping in a bed (a source that makes the night go by), by eating or drinking something (a food row), or any other way through a Trigger rule with the action "Raise a need" (near a fire, on a bench, at an altar). Switched off (its "On" box unticked), it has no bar, no longer goes down and no longer hurts; the bed and the coffee say it is switched off.
  • Aiming while building: the Building system's setting "How the player aims" follows the game's camera (the centre of the screen in first or third person, the cursor from above or from a placed camera), or forces one of them.
  • Interiors keep their light: the Day and night system has a setting for scenes without the cycle (a cave, an inn).
  • Large worlds: resources and built pieces stay in the game, asleep when far away; a tree chopped at the other end of the map still grows back on time.
  • Every setting is detailed in the systems reference.

items.title: The terrain
items.text: Without a terrain, a scene's ground is made of your objects (a large plane, tiles). A terrain is a map with relief, regions (forest, beach, snow...), water and vegetation, which you generate, then touch up with brushes.

items.title: Generating a world
items.text:
Deselect everything (or click the game row, at the very top of the Scene tab): the properties show the Terrain section. Set it up, then click Generate a world.

Setting Effect Size The side of the square map: 256 m, 512 m, 1,024 m, 2 km or 4 km (see Large maps). Relief 0: almost flat. 1: hills and mountains. 2: very steep. Relief details How many bumps and hollows there are between the large shapes (0 to 1). Max. altitude The height of the highest peaks, with a relief of 1. Coast level Below this share of the altitude: beaches and swamps, which water will cover. Shape Land to the edge, One continent, Several continents or Archipelago: land up to the edge of the map, or surrounded by a sea that reaches the horizon. Sea A sea at coast level: it covers everything lower. Always there around continents or islands. Seamless edges The left edge continues the right one, the top continues the bottom: a map that can one day wrap around the world. (The game does not cross from one edge to the other yet.) Regions Snow, Rock, Forest, Grassland, Desert, Swamp, Beach. Uncheck the ones you don't want: their areas take the most fitting neighboring region. A map keeps at least one region. Variant A number: the same variant gives the same world. The Another variant arrow draws one at random.

The terrain becomes the scene's Terrain object, with its regions and water stored inside. Objects already placed are set again on the new relief.

With a terrain, this section is called Relief, regions and sea (on the Terrain object) and its button Generate again: it replaces the relief and regions, but region objects keep their name, color and systems. Remove the terrain deletes it. Ctrl+Z goes back in both cases.

items.title: Importing a relief
items.text:
Import a relief (in the same section) makes the map from a heightmap: a grayscale image where white is the highest, like relief tools (World Machine, Gaea) and real-data converters make.

  • Files: a PNG image, preferably 16-bit (65,536 heights instead of 256: no steps on gentle slopes), or a raw .raw or .r16 file (16-bit heights, no header, in PC byte order; .r8 for 8-bit). The image must be square.
  • The box that follows shows the image ("1025 × 1025 points, 16-bit") and asks how to lay it out:
Setting Effect Meters per point The distance between two points of the image: 1,025 points at 1 m make a 1,024 m map. A map is at most 4 km per side. Black altitude The altitude of the image's black points, in meters. White altitude The altitude of its white points.
  • Import lays out the relief. Regions and sea follow the Generate a world settings (the checked regions, the coast level, the sea, the variant), as for a generated world. Placed objects are set again on the new relief, and Ctrl+Z brings back the old terrain.
  • An image whose number of cells (its points minus one) is not a multiple of 64 is resampled: the map keeps its size in meters.

items.title: Large maps (2 and 4 km)
items.text:
Beyond 1,024 m, the map is a large map. It is set up, sculpted and painted like the others; only the way it is drawn changes:

  • The ground is drawn in detail around the camera: up to 1 km in High quality, 500 m in Low quality (the quality is chosen from the graphics card). Further away, a simplified relief (one height every 4 m, its colors to within 4 m) takes over. As the camera moves, the detail loads little by little, without stutter.
  • Generating a 4 km map takes a few seconds.
  • In game, the ground is touched in 256 m squares, as a single piece: the player and characters cross from one to the next without noticing.

On every map, the relief is simplified in the distance: each 64 m piece is drawn with 64, 32, 16, 8 or 4 tiles per side, depending on how much of the screen it covers. It only changes detail when the relief's difference stays under one point of the screen (one and a half in Low quality): the difference cannot be seen. Under the edges of each piece, a skirt (a vertical strip of ground, normally invisible) fills the cracks that would open between two levels of detail.

items.title: The Terrain object
items.text:
Select Terrain in the scene list (or click the ground, or Edit the terrain in the game's settings). Its properties:

  • Position and size: the terrain moves, but does not turn or change scale;
  • Relief, regions and sea: the generation settings above;
  • Regions: New region creates a region of your own, to paint wherever you like (name it, give it its color and systems). The new object is selected, and the Paint tool taken;
  • Blend between regions: the width of the blend from one region to the next (0: sharp borders);
  • Systems: a system placed on the Terrain applies to all its regions.

items.title: Sculpting and painting
items.text:
With a terrain in the scene, the tool column on the left of the view shows seven tools: Hill, Dig, Flatten, Smooth, Ramp, Paint, Fill. With a tool taken, the left click in the view sculpts instead of selecting. Each tool and its options bar (Size, Strength, Region) are detailed in The 3D view.

  • While sculpting, slopes too steep for the player show in red.
  • Ramp: drag from one point to another for a path with an even slope.
  • Fill: click at the bottom of a hollow; water fills it up to its rim and becomes a Lake ("Lake created: its surface is at 12 m"). Nothing fills if the water would run off: dig a hollow first.
  • Each brush stroke is undone with Ctrl+Z. Esc puts the tool down.
  • Materials: cover the ground with real materials (grass, rock, snow, sand...) and paint them with the brush. See Materials.

items.title: Regions
items.text:
Each region is an object stored in the Terrain, with a dot of its color in the list. In the view, a first click on the ground selects the Terrain, a second the region under the mouse. Its properties:

  • what it covers ("23% of the map");
  • Regions: Paint this region takes the Paint tool with it;
  • Vegetation: see below;
  • Appearance: its Color;
  • Systems: they apply to what stands in it. For example the Sounds system and its surface setting: footsteps that crunch on snow.

Deleting a region (Del key) asks which region will take its areas ("Its areas will take this region:"). Its object goes with its systems; Ctrl+Z brings everything back. The terrain keeps at least one region.

items.title: Water
items.text:
The Sea and each Lake are objects stored in the Terrain. They cover what is lower than their level.

  • Style: Realistic (fine waves, reflections, see-through water) or Stylized, for a low poly game (see below).
  • Kind of water: a ready-made water, Sea, Stormy sea, Lagoon, Lake, Pond, Low poly sea or Low poly lake: the swell, the colors, the clarity and the foam at once (the last two also switch to the Stylized style). Everything stays adjustable afterwards.
  • Level: the height of the surface. Higher, the water covers more land.
  • Waves: the height of the largest waves. 0: calm water, like a mirror.
  • Wave length: from one crest to the next. Short, a chop; long, an ocean swell. Shorter waves are always added on top.
  • Swell direction: where the waves go, in degrees.
  • Choppiness: the wind on the water, from 0 (round, regular waves) to 1 (sharp crossing crests, foam).
  • Deep water color and Color near the shores: the water goes from one to the other with its depth.
  • Clarity: how far one sees through the water. Near the shores the bottom shows; further out it fades into the water's color.
  • Foam: on the crests, along the shores and around whatever touches the water (a rock, a pier, a floating crate).
  • Wakes: the V opening behind a boat, the churned water in its wake, the rings around a swimmer or a floating crate. They are only drawn. 0: none.
  • Systems: they apply to whoever walks in it (splashing steps).

Water reflects the sky, the sun and the scene's lights (a lamp by a lake draws its reflection on it); in High quality it also reflects the scenery, shows the bottom slightly bent by the waves, and the sun draws moving light patterns on it (caustics). The waves move with game time: what you see is what physics makes float.

In deep enough water, the player swims, at its Swim speed (in its properties): they follow the surface, rise and fall with it, and moving water gently carries them along. Del removes a body of water.

items.title: Stylized water
items.text:
For a low poly game, choose the Stylized style: the surface is made of flat facets, triangles laid on a fixed grid of the world, lifted by gentler, more readable waves; each facet takes its shade from its slope facing the sun. The colors go from the Color near the shores to the Deep water color in crisp steps, the foam lines the shores and whatever touches the water with a crisp band, the highest crests turn white and wakes are drawn as foam lines. The water reflects the sky and the sun (as a crisp spot), not the scenery, and shows the bottom without bending it. Its extra settings:

  • Facet size: the side of the triangles, in meters. Large, very low poly water; small, more detail.
  • Facet strength: at 1, each facet has its own shade; toward 0, the surface smooths out, with the same waves.
  • Color steps: the number of shades from the shore to the open water (0 or 1: a smooth gradient).
  • Foam width: the width of the white band along the shores and around objects.

The style does not depend on the render quality: stylized water stays stylized on a powerful computer. The quality only sets its cost: in High, a second foam band comes and goes beyond the first, and placed lights draw their reflection on it; in Low, the sea has a coarser mesh. At equal quality, stylized water costs less than realistic water. Floating and swimming things follow the drawn facets.

items.title: Rivers
items.text: The Source tool (in the tool column, under Lake) puts a water source with one click on the terrain: its river runs down the slope by itself, fills hollows into lakes, digs its bed and stops in the sea, in a lake or at the map edge. Its options bar sets the Flow (a stream, a river, a wide river) and the Current. The River is an object stored in the Terrain: Delete removes it, and the ground comes back as it was.

items.title: Editing the course by hand
items.text:
Click the water of a river (or its line in the scene list): it shows its handles in the view, whatever tool is taken.

Handle What it does The drop The source. Drag it: the river is made again from there. A round handle A waypoint. Drag it: the river passes where you put it. A click selects it (a mint ring), Delete removes it. A plus In the middle of each stretch of the course. A click adds a waypoint there; drag it to put it somewhere else.
  • The handle under the mouse, or the one you hold, is mint. The river is made again when you release the mouse.
  • Between two points, the river keeps its natural path. Where the ground rises, WorldMint digs the bed through: water never flows uphill.
  • A point that needs too deep a cut (more than Deepest cut, 10 m at first), that is in water or outside the map, or that would make the river run back over itself, turns orange for a few seconds, and a sentence says why, in the status bar and on the handle. The river then keeps its course.
  • Ctrl+Z undoes each gesture, one by one; Ctrl+Y redoes it.

In Properties, the River section sets the Flow, the Bed width, the Bed depth, the Current and the Deepest cut; Back to the natural course removes all your waypoints. The look of the water (style, colours, foam) is set just below, as for a lake.

items.title: Editing a lake by hand
items.text:
Click the water of a lake (or its line in the scene list): its shore shows its handles in the view, at the height of the water, with a thin line along the shore.

Handle What it does A round handle A point of the shore. Drag it: the lake grows or shrinks up to there. A click selects it (a mint ring), Delete removes it (3 points at least). A plus In the middle of each side. A click adds a point there; drag it to put it somewhere else.
  • The shore passes smoothly through the points, without corners. When you release the mouse, WorldMint makes the bottom again: a gently sloping shore, deeper in the middle. Around it, higher ground slopes down to the water and lower ground is raised by an embankment: the water stays inside the shore, it neither overflows nor floats.
  • Where the lake shrinks, the old bottom is filled up to the water level: it becomes a meadow, not a dry hole.
  • A point outside the map, or a shore that would cross itself, or reach into the sea or another lake, turns orange for a few seconds, and a sentence says why. The lake then keeps its shape.
  • Ctrl+Z undoes each gesture, one by one; Ctrl+Y redoes it.

In Properties, the Lake section sets the Depth at the deepest point; the Level, lower down with the look of the water, raises or lowers the surface, and the bottom and banks follow. A lake made with the bucket has no handles yet: Edit the shore by hand gives it some, on its current shore.

items.title: Editing the coast by hand
items.text:
Select the sea (its line in the scene list, or a click on the water), bring the view close to the shore to change, then, in Properties, Coast section, click Edit the coast by hand: a line of 7 points is laid on the shore nearest the centre of the view.

Handle What it does A round handle A point of the line. Drag it: the coast passes where you put it. Out to sea, the land moves forward; inland, the sea comes in as a bay. A click selects it, Delete removes it (2 points at least). A plus In the middle of each stretch. A click adds a point there; drag it to put it somewhere else.
  • When you release the mouse, WorldMint digs below the water on the sea side and builds up above it on the land side, over 40 m on each side of the line, gently sloping (Beach slope, 0.08 at first: a sandy beach). Further away, the ground comes back as it was, smoothly; both ends of the line stay anchored, and the rest of the map does not change.
  • Each gesture starts again from the ground as it was before the line: moving a point and putting it back gives the original coast.
  • A point outside the map, or a line that would cross itself, turns orange for a few seconds and a sentence says why; the coast keeps its shape.
  • Ctrl+Z undoes each gesture. Put the coastline here replaces the line with a new one, near the centre of the view. The sea Level is set as before: the beach along the line follows.

items.title: What floats
items.text: Water carries what moves: the objects of the Physics system float, sink or stay in between, by their In water setting; the water slows them down, rocks them with the waves and carries them when it moves. The pieces of a broken object do the same, and a rag doll floats. A boat sails on it and runs aground on land. The fluid is not simulated: the water's surface carries things, which stays light for the computer.

items.title: Vegetation
items.text:
To grow trees, bushes, grass or rocks on a region:

  1. Select the region.
  2. Drag a model from the library onto the area of the Vegetation section ("Drop a model from the explorer here: it will grow on this region.").

The model becomes a plant kind, an object stored in the region, and grows over the whole region. Drag other models to grow several kinds. The region's Vegetation section lists its kinds and their number of plants; a click selects one.

A plant kind's properties ("It grows on its region. Its settings and systems apply to all its plants."):

Setting Effect Density The number of plants per 100 m². Changing the density resows: hand edits may no longer land on the same plants. Min. size, Max. size Each plant takes a random size between the two. Max. slope Nothing grows on steeper ground. Sink into the ground Each plant rests on the lowest ground under its base, then sinks this much: its base seems to come out of the ground. Visible up to Beyond this, it is not drawn: closer makes the game faster. In Low quality (an integrated chip), plants stop at 60 % of this distance. Sway in the wind How much its plants bend in the wind (set in Sky and light), from 0 (stiff) to 1 (the most supple grass). Auto: from the model's height, grass very supple, a big tree a little and more slowly. Grounds On which ground materials its plants grow. By default, on the terrain's natural grounds (those of its regions and rules, and the shipped grounds): a square of tiles or paving painted by hand stays bare. For each material: Grows here (where it is painted, only on the ticked grounds) or Never (painted or not). Reseed New places for all its plants. Hand edits are forgotten. Trunk (In game section) The diameter that stops the player in the game. 0: walked through (grass, flowers, bushes).
  • Select all its plants: to edit them or give them a system together.
  • Put all plants back: forgets the hand edits (if there are any).
  • Stop growing it: removes this plant kind.
  • A system placed on the plant kind applies to all its plants: for example Gathering, for trees to chop down.

items.title: Editing a plant
items.text:
A plant is selected with a click in the view, or in the scene list, under its plant kind (with the word "plant"). Ctrl + click and the rectangle take several. It is not a scene object, but it is edited like one and keeps its edit if the terrain changes:

  • Position, Rotation, Size, or the gizmo;
  • Place on ground (End);
  • Put back in place: as sown, with its original place, rotation and size;
  • Erase (Del): it will not grow back, even if the terrain changes;
  • Make it an object: it leaves its plant kind and becomes a scene object, in the same place. Not needed to give it a system;
  • Select its plant kind;
  • Systems: a plant can carry its own systems, and stays a plant.

items.title: Translating your game
items.text: You write your game in your language. To offer it in English, Spanish or German as well, add these languages and fill in their translations: yourself, cell by cell, or the agent, in one click. No code is needed.

items.title: Choosing the game's languages
items.text:
With nothing selected in the scene, the properties show the game settings. In the Game languages section:

  • Original language: the language you write the lines, the messages and the title in. Usually yours.
  • Add a language: each added language is offered to players. The cross next to a language removes it; its translations stay in the project, and adding it back finds them again.

The agent can do it too: "put my game in English and Spanish".

items.title: Which language the player sees
items.text:
When it starts, the game picks the player's language:

  1. the one they chose last time in the menu options;
  2. otherwise the Windows language, if the game offers it (a Canadian English Windows gives English);
  3. otherwise the original language.

With the Menu system, the Options button shows a Language row: each click moves to the next language, and everything on screen updates. The game remembers it for the next plays.

A text without a translation shows in the original language: a half-translated game stays playable.

items.title: The Translations window
items.text:
The Game > Translations menu (or the Translations... button of the game languages) opens the list of every text the player sees, found automatically:

  • the systems' texts: the lines and answers of the Dialogue, a character's displayed name, the messages and ending text of the Trigger, the title-screen title of the Menu, an Interaction prompt's text, the item kinds of the Inventory, the resources, tools and verbs of Harvesting, a Shop's name, money and items, the titles, descriptions, steps and rewards of the Quest log;
  • the systems' own texts: "Play" and "Options" of the Menu, "Buy" of the Shop, "Quest log", "Map"... The Where column says "system text". They already exist in French and English: their cell shows that text in grey, and the game shows it until you write another one. In the other languages, they wait for their translation like the others;
  • the game's title, and the names of the controls you named;
  • the scripts' texts written with game.t("...").

There is one column per offered language. A red cell is waiting for its translation: click it, type, then press Enter. At the top, each language says how many texts it still lacks; Only what is missing hides the ones already translated. The Where column says where each text appears. A changed translation is undone with Ctrl+Z (and comes back with Ctrl+Y), like any change in the editor.

items.title: Asking the agent
items.text:
The Ask the agent to translate button sends a request to the agent: it reads the missing texts, translates them keeping the game's tone, and fills in the tables. The cells fill in before your eyes; you can then correct any of them.

Formatting stays

A text like [b]Garde[/b] or Il faut : {outil} keeps its tags and marks in its translation: [b]Guard[/b], You need: {outil}. The agent knows it; if you translate yourself, copy them.

items.title: Where translations are stored
items.text:
Each offered language has its table in the project, in the translations folder: translations/en.json for English, translations/es.json for Spanish. One line per text: the text as written in the game, then its translation.

{
  "Bonjour, voyageur.": "Hello, traveller.",
  "Halte !": "Halt!"
}

The file can be read and corrected with any text editor, and compares well in Git. If you change an original text, its translation does not follow: it shows in red again in the Translations window.

The exported game takes these tables with it.

items.title: For scripts
items.text: A script passes every text it shows through game.t: game.hud_text("score", game.t("Coins: {1}", coins)). {1}, {2}... are replaced after the translation, so the word order can change from one language to another. The systems' texts are already translated. The scripts reference details game.language, game.languages and game.set_language.

items.title: The Trigger: "when… then…"
items.text:
The Trigger system makes the game react without writing code. You place rules on an object that read like a sentence: when the player steps on this plate, then the door opens. They are all set in the object's Properties, and the agent can place them for you.

Every field is detailed in the Trigger reference.

items.title: Placing a rule
items.text:
1. Activate the system: the Developer mode's Systems panel, Activate under Trigger (see The game's systems and settings).
  2. Place it on the object the rule is about (the plate, the lever, the boss): drag Trigger from the library's Systems folder onto the object, or, in its Properties, Systems section, click + System.
  3. In the object's Properties, under Trigger, click Add: Rule. A Rule 1 appears, in its own frame; the cross on its right removes it. An object can carry as many rules as needed.
  4. Choose When, then Then, then fill in the fields that appear: only those useful for the chosen action are shown.

Every change goes through the history: Ctrl+Z undoes it.

items.title: When
items.text:
When What the object needs Someone enters this zone (Zone system) The Zone system: see Physics and zones. Someone leaves this zone (Zone system) The Zone system. The player uses it (Interaction system) The Interaction system: the player walks up to it and presses its key (E at first). It dies (Health system) The Health system. When the game starts Nothing. After a time Nothing: you give the number of seconds of play. When an event happens Nothing: you give the event's name, one of a system (see The events) or a name chosen for this game. Its joint breaks (Joint system) The Joint system, with a breaking force or the Break action.

How many times: Only once, or Every time. With After a time and Every time, the action comes back every so many seconds.

Wait before acting (seconds): a delay between the moment the rule fires and the action. A door that closes three seconds after the player went through.

items.title: Then
items.text:
Then What it does Show an object, Hide an object A hidden object can no longer be seen and no longer stops anyone: a hidden door is an open door. Show or hide, in turn Each time, the opposite of the time before: a lever that opens, then closes. Switch a light on, Switch a light off, Switch a light on or off, in turn A placed light: a lever that lights a lamp. Change a light's color It takes the New color of the light: an alarm turning red. Destroy an object Removes it from the game (never the player). Make a copy appear Copies the chosen object, at the place chosen in Where it appears. The copied object is usually a hidden model, kept aside. Teleport the player to an object The player ends up where that object is. Make solid, Make passable A passable object stays visible but no longer stops anyone. On a zone: switches it back on, or off. Go to another scene The player goes to the chosen Scene, at its Arrival point. End the game Victory or Defeat, with a Text to show; the game offers to play again. Play a sound A sound from the library, played where the object is. Play a video A video from the library, full screen, with its sound; the world stops meanwhile. The player can skip it or not; Event sent at the end chains what comes next. See Videos. Play an effect (fire, chips, explosion…), Stop an effect Lights again the effect the target carries (its Particle effect system: a brazier lit by a lever), or plays a ready-made effect on it, once, at the chosen Size of the effect; Stop an effect puts it out. See Particles and decals. Muffle the sound (under water, behind a wall) Muffles a group of the sound mixer, or all the game's sound, from 0 (clear again) to 1 (under water), over a few seconds. Mute or unmute a group of sounds Silences a group of the sound mixer (the ambience during a story scene), or brings it back. Music: play one over the background music, Music: back to the background music A music for a moment (a boss, a chase, a quest step): the Sounds module's background music fades down without stopping, then resumes where it is on the way back, asked by another rule (on an event, the end of a step) or, without Looping, at the end of the piece.
